SPROULE (East Grey) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 64) to amend the Dominion Lands Act. He said:	This
Bill is to correct what appears to have been an error which crept into the Bill as it passed last year. When the Dominion Lands Bill was before the Senate on July 17, 1908 -three days before the closing of parliament-an amendment was there moved to the following effect as appears by the minutes of the Senate:
The order of the day being read for the third reading of Bill (No. 181) entitled an Act to consolidate and amend the Acts respecting the public lands of the Dominion, as amended, the Hon. Mr. Scott moved, seconded by the Right Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright, that the said Bill, as amended, be now read a third time. The Hon. Mr. Lougheed in amendment, moved, seconded by Hon. Mr. Perley:
That the said Bill be not now read a third time but be amended by restoring to section 42 in the 6th line thereof before the word ' schools,' the word ' public ' so as to read ' public schools ', as now in the present law respecting Dominion lands. The question of concurrence being put thereon, the same was resolved in the affirmative. The question of concurrence being again put on the main motion, the same was resolved in the affirmative. The said Bill, as further amended, was then read a third time accordingly. The question was put whether this Bill as further amended, shall pass. This was resolved in the affirmative.
Ordered, that the clerk go down to the House of Commons and acquaint that House that the Senate have passed this Bill with several amendments to which they desire their concurrence.

The message was taken down to the House of Commons on the same day, as appears from the Votes and Proceedings, July 17, 1908, page 1454. The minute is as follows:
A message was received from the Senate agreeing to the Bill (No. 181) to consolidate and amend the Acts respecting the public lands of the Dominion with an amendment which is as follows:
Page 8, line 21-after ' provide ' insert the following as subclause 9 of clause 15:
' Every one is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to two years imprisonment, who buys, trades or sells, or professes to buy trade or sell land, or any interest in or control of land open to homestead entry, or for which homestead entry has been - granted, before patent therefor has been issued.
The House then adjourned at 1.55 o'clock a.m. until 11 o'clock a.m. this day.
It will be seen that the amendment moved by Senator Lougheed and adopted by the Senate did not appear in the message sent to the House of Commons and therefore that amendment did not come before the House for concurrence. Who was responsible for this omission, and whether it was the result of accident or design is to me unknown. In any event it never came before this House. This House agreed to the one amendment sent down, as appears from the following entry in our Votes and Proceedings of July 18 last, page 1464:
The amendments made by the Senate to the following Bills were taken into consideration and agreed to, namely Bill (No. 189) to amend the Civil Service Act, and Bill (No. 181) to consolidate and amend the Act respecting the public lands of the Dominion.
The result is that the clause, as it now stands, in the statutes of 1908, materially changes the law, as the word ' public ' is omitted and the words now are: ' organized and carried on in accordance with the law of such province.
That was a material change in the Act. And, right here, I wish to draw attention to another thing. When the first Dominion Lands Bill was brought down, it had explanatory notes after the several clauses. The clause to which I now refer contained an amendment which appears in the Bill of 1908, and the note at the foot of it refers only to another amendment of the law which was properly brought to our attention by that explanatory note. But, when the Bill of the succeeding year was brought down, which purports to have the same explanatory notes at the foot of each clause, and where this important amendment was made_ in that clause, there is no reference to it in the explanatory note, but there is a reference to another change which was made in that clause. It was clause 42. In the Act of 1906-7, the clause is practically the same as in the old law and provides as follows :
All moneys from time to time realized from the sale of school lands should be invested in Mr. SPROULE.
securities of Canada to form a school fund and the interest arising therefrom, after deducting the cost of management, should be paid annually to the government of the province within which such lands are situate toward the support of public schools therein.
The explanatory note says:
This provision is the same as in the present law, except that the words ' or territory ' have been struck out, as the territory referred to has been divided into the new provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, and there are no school lands beyond.
In the Bill of 1908, in which the important amendment I have referred to is made, there is no explanatory clause, except the one in the former Bill which I have just read. It makes no reference to the other very important ohajige introduced into this Bill of 1908. Therefore reading the explanatory notes, as one naturally would, and finding no statement to the effect that this important change was to be made, in all human probability, a few of the members, when the Bill was going through, read the clause as it is now in the law. The Bill which I now introduce is to amend the Act so as to make it read as it was heretofore. The section now reads:
All moneys from time to time realized from the sale of school lands should be invested in securities of Canada to form a school fund, and the interest arising therefrom, after deducting the cost of management, should be paid annually to the government of the province within which such lands are situate, towards the support of schools organized and carried on in accordance with the law of such province.
The words of the old law were:
-toward the support of public schools therein.
My amendment would restore the wording of the original clause before this amendment was made in 1908.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

TURRIFF (Assiniboia) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 65) to amend the Railway Act. He said: Mr. Speaker, this Bill is, word for word, the Bill I promoted in this House last year. The Bill, after being introduced and read the first and second times, was sent to the Railway Committee, and there amended into the shape in which it now is. It passed the Railway Committee and came to this House, but was so late in getting through the Railway Committee that the session ended before it could be reached. The Bill provides that every railway company that receives a charter from this parliament shall be compelled not to spend fifteen per cent within the first two years as provided by the present law, but shall be compelled, if the railway is under 250 miles in length, to build ten per cent of the mileage during the first

two years, an additional ten per cent in the third year, another ten in the fourth year, and to complete the road in five years as at present; if the road is over 250 miles in length, the company shall be compelled to build at least one-twentieth of the mileage in the first two years, an additional one-twentieth in each of the third and fourth years, and to complete in five years as at present. I believe that something along this line is absolutely necessary. I speak with some experience of how these matters work out, in the western country at all events. The constituency I represent is an old-settled constituency-settled since 1882-and there are many settlers in that country who have been waiting year after year for a road to be built; charters have been granted eight or ten years ago, and yet nothing has been done toward extending ^these lines of railway. The companies come before this House and before the Railway Committee, and, on one excuse or another, they get an extension of time. We have seen it this year in the Railway Committee that, almost every time an effort is made to force a railway company to build so much of its line each year, the excuse is made: You cannot pick out one railway company and treat it differently from the others. I agree with that; it would not be fair to treat one differently from the others. But I believe that it would be in the interest of the country generally, and especially of the west, that all railway companies should be compelled to build a certain proportion of their roads every year or forfeit the charter. It has been stated, time and again, that the possession of a charter does not prevent another road from getting a charter and going on and building. That may be well enough in theory, but it does not work out that way in practice. When one big company has the charter, it can play the dog in the manger to the fullest extent, not building its own proposed road and yet preventing other railways from building. We have had that to contend with for years in my own constituency. One of the big companies, the Canadian Pacific Railway, has a charter. They will not build the road, but the moment the Canadian Northern, or the Grand Trunk Pacific, gets a charter, and proposes to build, the Canadian Pacific Railway will go on and grade a few miles. Only yesterday, in the Railway Committee an hon. member from British Columbia gave us an instance in which one of the big railway companies- the same company-in order to keep out the Jim Hill system graded a portion of the road and laid the rails, but as soon as they had shut out the building of a competing line they not only ceased working, but actually took up the rails they had already laid. Is that a state of things we ought to tolerate in this country? I claim that the time has come when some change ought to be made. The railway companies are doing exactly as they like. We have no say as to where they
shall build the branch lines; in the western country at all events they do not consult the wishes of the people, but build with a view to cutting out competing companies. What we want is a law that will compel them, when they get a charter, to go on and do something with the road. I have understood my right hon. friend the leader of the government (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) to state on several occasions that whenever the Railway Committee take a certain line of action, it is not his policy or the policy of the government to go contrary to the wishes of that committee.
I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Turriff) should confine himself to an explanation of his Bill as is customary on the first reading.

Well, those, Mr. Speaker, are the reasons I have for introducing this Bill, and those are the provisions of the Bill. If it is thought desirable to send it to the Railway Committee. I have not the slightest doubt that the Railway Com mittee will do again this year as it did last year, pass the Bill and send it back here to be dealt with by the House.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speechtext: -FISHERIES IN NEW BRUNSWICK.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. W. DANIEL (St. John City).
speechtext:
I would like to call the attention of the government, and especially of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to a statement which I see in the St. John ' Globe ' of February 17. This is the statement :
In an Ottawa despatch to the Fredericton * Gleaner * the position of the New Brunswick government is defined. Hon. Mr. Grimmer, Surveyor General, who represents this province at the conference, says:
' While he had no official knowledge of the nature of the proposed regulations he had been given to understand that they were applied to spawning grounds in the waters of Grand Manan and Petit Manan, and other points in New Brunswick sea waters which were fifteen miles and more from the international boundaries. He could not see how these could be described as international waters, and could see no reason for Canada's handing the management of them over to a Mr. MURPHY.
commission in which the United States had anv say.'
But this is the part to which I wish particularly to call attention :
In the original draft, as he understood it, it was proposed to give to the fishermen of each nation the right to come in and fish in the waters of the other nations as they were covered by the joint commission. He did not know how far this had been modified by the later changes in the regulations, but if it were put in force in that form it would hand over to Americans the best fishing grounds in Canada, while the American waters which were thrown open to Canadian were not worth mentioning. What he objected to was the principle of declaring waters to be international which were nowhere near the boundary line.
I would like to know from the government whether it is a fact that the treaty, and the regulations which are to be made under it, will permit American fishermen to enjoy the privileges of our inland fisheries in any of the waters which are embraced in this treaty; because if it does, it would allow American fishermen to come into the harbour of St. John and carry on fishing operations there, and fish all the way up the St. John river, notwithstanding that the harbour and the greater part of the river and many miles away from the boundary. I think it very important that the public should know whether that is the intention or not.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. P. BRODEUR (Minister of Marine and Fisheries).
speechtext: In virtue of the treaty which was signed last year, it is provided that the fishery regulations of some of the boundary waters shall be uniform and under the control of a joint commission appointed by the Canadian government and the American government. This commission is composed of Dr. Jordan, as was stated the other day, on the American side, and Dr. Prince on the Canadian side. They are now at work preparing the regulations. I understand that a draft which has been prepared by the American commissioner got abroad and was published. I do not know whether the draft as published is correct or not. I am inclined to believe that it is not correct. At all events this draft has not been accepted by our commissioner and the regulations are the subject of negotiations now between the American and Canadian commissioners.

If the minister will excuse me, I think he did not answer the question which I asked whether the treaty, or these regulations would permit alien or American fishermen to fish in Canadian waters which are included in the treaty.
I missed that point. It is formally stated in the treaty, if I remember it aright, that Canadians will have the exclusive right to fish on the Canadian side and Americans on the American side.
That is a very important statement, and if that is so I presume that Americans will have the right to come into St. John harbour and fish
No, no.
It is the other way.

No, my hon. friend did not understand me aright. I said that Canadians would have the right to fish on the Canadian side and Americans on the American side. There is no proposition, and I understand it will be contrary to the treaty for the Commission to give to American fishermen the right to fish in Canadian waters.
May I ask the minister one further question as to who will have the ultimate ratification or approval of these regulations made or to be made by Professor Prince and Mr. Jordan?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The two governments.
With or without the knowledge of parliament?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I cannot say as to that, but I may state that some fifteen or sixteen years ago the American and Canadian governments had a commission to make regulations for the preservation of fish in boundary waters. They made a report suggesting certain close seasons and joint regulations to be approved by both countries. This report never was acted upon by the American government, although we are prepared to act upon it. The object of the present commission is to have a system of joint regulations applicable both in the United States and in Canada so far as close seasons and other matters are concerned, but neither country has surrendered its rights within its own waters.
May I ask as to whether this treaty goes into effect without being presented to the Canadian parliament?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think it does.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to ask the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) a question which I must preface by a few words. I noticed by the press yesterday that regulations are now being framed under the provisions of the Waterways Treaty, and I understand that these regulations simply refer to international waters. Under the decision of the Privy Council in the fisheries case some years ago, or by virtue of that decision, there has occurred and is occurring a conflict between the federal and provincial governments respecting their several jurisdictions. Some year or two ago, I think, the government appointed one Mr. Bastedo, of the province
of Ontario, as a commissioner to negotiate with the provinces and to obtain, if possible some settlement or understanding as to the extent of the jurisdiction of the provinces and of the federal authorities. I noticed by the press lately that Mr. Bastedo was removed from this position and that Professor Prince was appointed in his place. I would like to know if Professor Prince is carrying on the negotiations with the provincial governments, if he has reported progress and what, if any, information the Minister of Marine and Fisheries can give us. It is an extremely important matter and it is a very unfortunate thing for the fisheries of this country that, by reason of the decision of the Privy Council, there exists a conflict of jurisdiction. As far as the province of Nova Scotia is concerned, I am sure it would be quite willing to abandon any rights it may have as a province under that decision and transfer them to the Dominion government. I believe that in that province we would go as far as to amend the British North America Act to make it absolutely plain

I am afraid that the hon. gentleman is exceeding the limits of a question.
. ^r- K; MACLEAN. I am just finishes make it absolutely plain that the control of our coast fisheries is absolutely within the control of the Dominion parliament. The question I desire to ask is what progress has been made with the negotiations with the provinces respecting this matter?

There have been no negotiations with the provincial governments concerning the question of the fisheries except in a casual way in a conference which took place a few days ago between representatives of the New Brunswick, Quebec and Ontario governments and myself. As there may be some misapprehension with reeard to that conference, I may inform the House as to what has been done and as to the circumstances under which that conference took place. This conference had nothing to do with the Waterways Commission, as my hon. friend has stated, but it was held for the purpose of discussing with the provincial governments interested, that is to say, the governments of New Brunswick, Quebec and Ontario, the regulations which are to be the subject of negotiations between the Canadian and American commissioners. I thought that before the Canadian commissioner should meet more formally the American commissioner he should have the benefit of the views of the provincial authorities. The three governments in question were, with the exception of the government of British Columbia, the only ones which were interested in the regulations which are to be made under the

treaty. The treaty provides for joint and uniform regulations in Passamaquoddy bay and in the St. John and St. Croix rivers in the province of New Brunswick; in Lake Memphramagog and Lake Champlain, in the province of Quebec, and within the great lakes and connecting rivers in Ontario, including the north channel. I thought that before Professor Prince should meet the American commissioner he should have the opportunity of meeting and consulting with the provincial authorities as to the regulations which should be accepted. The conference took place; while I am not at liberty to state what has been the result of this conference, I must say that it was conducted in the most harmonious way, and that we were very glad to have the benefit of the views which were expressed by the provincial governments.
That is hardly an answer to my question. What I want to know is this: Some two years ago the government was in conference with the provincial governments as to the question of jurisdiction
The rules only allow the hon. gentleman to ask a question.
There were no negotiations with regard to the question of the jurisdiction of the provincial authorities except in a casual way at the conference which took place the other day.
Are the negotiations still going on?

With reference to the regulations which are to be made by Professor Prince and Mr. Jordan and on which the minister has asked the views of representatives from the provincial governments, would he take occasion to consult with the members of the House before these regulations are finally adopted?
I will be very glad to have the benefit of the views of the members of the House who take an interest in the matter; in fact I have already asked some hon. gentlemen to give me their views.
The regulations to be made would cover the whole of the St. John river ?
Yes.

I understood the hon. gentleman to sav that the finding of these commissioners would not require to be ratified by parliament. Will the government have power to accept or reject that conclusion if they think fit ?

Yes.

I would like to ask the minister if, under the terms of the treaty, all the waters of the St. John river and its tributaries are placed under the control of the International Commission, or is the jurisdiction limited to the portion of the waters which constitute the boundary line?
If I remember aright, the treaty includes the whole of the St. John river; the part in Canada as well as the part in the United States.
And all its tributaries ?
The tributaries are not included.

As the minister has given us an opinion on two or three occasions as to what the treaty really means in certain points, I would ask him whether it is not competent for the government to make all the members of the House quite as wise as himself by laying that treaty on the table of the House.
It was laid on the table of the House last year.

I wish to call attention to what appears to be an inaccuracy in the reply given to-day to question No. 20 on the Order Paper. _ I asked whether this government had received from the government of British Columbia a certain resolution, and the answer was, no. I have in my hand a report of the proceeding's of the British Columbia legislature on the 2nd inst., in which appears this communication from the secretary of the Lieutenant Governor of the province:
The 28th day of January, 1909.
At the Government House, Victoria, B.C.
Pear Sir.-In reply to your memorandum, of the 27th inst., with regard to a resolution having reference to oriental immigration, which was forwarded by His Honour to Ottawa on the 16th March last, the only correspondence thereon received from the Secretary of State was a letter-dated the 23rd of March, informing His Honour that it had been submitted to His Excellency the Governor General in Council.
In view of this I would like to ask if the Secretary of State would be good enough to inquire further into the matter and give me a more complete answer to the question.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I presume that the Secretary of State answered from the information given him by his department, but I have already asked my private secretary to look through the correspondence of the Privy Council Department and I presume it may be found there.

I want to ask the Minister of Marine and Fisheries a question which was put by me on Monday and Tuesday last, and which was put by the hon. the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Borden) on Wednesday. Why is it that the fishermen in a number of the districts in Halifax county have not yet received the blank forms on which to file their claims for last year's bounty ? This is an important matter and I wish an answer.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. P. BRODEUR (Minister of Marine and Fisheries).
speechtext: I was engaged on Tuesday and Wednesday at the conference with reference to the fishery regulations and was unfortunately unable to be present in the House, but I can answer the hon. gentleman now. Formerly the bounty claims were collected by Mr. Ogden who was in charge of the Bedford fish hatchery and who resigned in July or August last. These bounty claims are generally collected after the fishing season which would be about the end of November. I do not think the appointment covers the whole county of Halifax. but there was delay with regard to the district between Bedford and Nine Mile river in which Mr. Ogden formerly collected the claims. On the 3rd of December I made a recommendation to council for the appointment of another man, at a small salary, I think $75, to look after the collection of these claims. That recommendation had to go to the treasury board and unfortunately it was lost between the Privy Council and the Treasury Board. When my attention was called to this later on I made a new recommendation, and the new man has been appointed and I am informed the collection is being made. All those who have claims for bounties will be paid as promptly as possible.
Am I to understand that this gentleman is in his office now and collecting claims? I am informed by some fishermen that they have not yet had an opportunity of filing their claims.
Mr. Venning informs me that Mr. Christian was fully instructed as to his duties and supplied with the necessary forms.
But they have not yet got to the fishermen ?
The fishermen will of course be paid later on.
When will the concluding volume of the Auditor General's Report be brought down ?
I expect it will be ready to-morrow.
When may we expect the report of the Department of Railways and Canals ?

speakeroldname: Hon. G. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals).
speechtext: Early next week; it is in the hands of the printer.

House in Committee of Supply.
Public buildings, chargeable to capital- Ottawa, new departmental buildings, $125,000.
['The first will be the Bill that stands in the name of the Minister of Justice. Then we will go into Supply, and continue with the estimates of the Public Works Department.']

speakeroldname: Hon. WM. PUGSLEY (Minister of Public Works).
speechtext: This sum is asked to make provision to complete payments for the purchase of properties on Sussex street and Mackenzie avenue as a site for the new departmental buildings. I gave very full information at the last session in regard to the cost of the land.

Has any additional land
been bought since?
Yes, and we have expropriated the remainder. Between the first of April, 1908, and the 31st of December there was paid $49,394.30. I cannot give the actual dates of the purchases.
These are payments which were made in carrying out the purchases which were agreed upon, and which were explained to the House last session?
Yes.
Has all the land been purchased and paid for that is necessary for these buildings?
No, not all paid for, because with respect to some of the properties, we have not been able to agree with the vendors, and proceedings have been taken in the Exchequer Court to obtain a valuation.
What is the total amount paid so far?
Up to the 31st December, 1908, $459,900.
What is the estimate of the amount required to secure the whole?
It isi expected that the present vote will cover the entire purchase.
That will make about $600,000?
Just about.
What is being done with reference to the buildings?

Nothing has been done with regard to the erection of the buildings beyond obtaining the plans; but I think it is not unlikely that in the very near future a start wiil be made, not for the erection of all the buildings, but for the erection of a wing to afford much needed accommodation. As the estimated cost of the buildings is very considerable, we have not thought it well to proceed with the whole scheme at the present time.
What is the estimated cost?
Is any portion of this to be devoted to building purposes?

I am not quite sure. It is just possible that if the expropriation valuation is not completed at a fairly early date, we may enter into a contract for the erection of a wing; and, if so, we will use part of the money for that purpose. I may say we are greatly pressed by the Board of Railway Commissioners for additional accommodation, and, instead of renting premises in Ottawa, we have thought it might be well to erect what would serve in the future as a wing of these buildings. I am not quite sure whether we shall do that or not; it is now under consideration.

I think my hon. friend would do well to add the words, ' purchase of site ' to this vote, so that he would not use a portion of it to commence a wing. Let it stand for what it is intended for. What does my hon.; friend think the wing will cost?

We have not yet had an estimate of the cost of the wing prepared. The chief architect is considering the matter. I may say that it is only within the last two or three weeks that it has been pressed on my attention by the Board of Railway Commissioners. They are greatly cramped for room, and they have asked us to rent a building to give them more accommodation. In considering what would be the necessary rental, I have thought that a good deal of money could be saved if we made a start by erecting a wing to afford the Railway Commissioners the accommodation they require, and to let the larger building stand for perhaps a fey years. But this is entirely tentative. It will be some little time before the chief architect can give us the plans and estimates of cost of the building.
Are the plans being prepared by the government architect ?

Plans have been received, as the result of public competition, but they are being revised by the government architect, and we are considering whether we might not, with great advan-Mr. FOSTER.
tage and economy, erect a wing which could be used for the Board of Railway Commissioners.
My hon. friend cannot build that out of this appropiation. He cannot really take anything out of this appropriation for that purpose.
We could let the contract.

Could you let a contract without having a sufficient amount of money voted, at least to carry on the operations for the year? The explanation of my hon. friend was that this would barely suffice to pay for the ground. We should have some definiteness if possible in our estimates. If this is for the purchase of a site, let it appear, and if my hon. friend proposes to go into the erection of a department building let him come down and ask for an appropriation. He may think it would be economy to build a wing, but I think he will admit that there are some other considerations to be looked at which might make it less desirable to go into any other large expenditure.

I have given every consideration to the matter. To arrange for the erection of a suitable building would mean the erection by a private company of a building suitable for the purpose, and that would mean engaging to rent the building for a term of years, to which I am opposed as it would not be economy to do so.
For what department is this?

For the Board of Rail-Commissioners. They are very much cramped now. Several clerks occupy one room, and some are in rooms which are very dark. Mr^ Scott, the assistant chief commissioner, has a room entirely unsuitable, and I think the demand is reasonable. What I thought might be done is this. It is possible that these properties, in regard to which proceedings have to be taken in the Exchequer Court, will not be required to be paid for until next year. If we have this vote, we could erect a suitable wing, or a part of a wing suitable for the accommodation required for $100,000, and it might be economy to let the contract and have the building completed next year.

When the minister was arranging for the building of these new departmental offices, did he consider the advisability of securing the block between the Post Office and the Langevin block? That is a block which the government could secure, and make that street opposite the parliamentary buildings all government property. In a few years that property will be much more valuable than now. I would like to see that building out there, or at least as much as could be used for a public building.

I have thought of that property, but as the government has such a large amount of property on Sussex street and Mackenzie avenue, I did not feel justified in entering into negotiations for its purchase at present.
Ottawa Parliament Buildings-additions and alterations, $93,000.
This is to provide for buildings during the coming year, the works in connection with the additions and alterations of the parliament buildings, such as the new wing and additions.
How much will that make the total cost of the new wing?
Including everything, $447,732.94. That will include the original contract, also the elevators, heating, plumbing, furniture, electric wiring, etc.
What was the amount of the original contract?
And the extras amount to as much more?

They are not extras. They are things which were not provided for in the original contract. They include taking down walls, cementing walls, the renewal of wings, lumber, hardware, elevators, $17,150, alterations and improvements in the different buildings, switchboards, radiators, etc.
Were not tenders invited for these additions? Were tenders invited for the elevators?

No, we decided that it is very much better to instal the Otis-Fensom elevator, as we believe their system to be the best. We have had some experience calling for tenders in elevators, and it was very unsatisfactory.
Which of these items, not included in the original contract, were given out without tender?
Then all the other $237,000 were given out without tender?
Without public tender.
What line of action was followed in deciding to whom these should be given?

The contractor for the building was asked to tender for the different works. It would be very much more convenient for him to do the other work; and upon his tender being received, the chief architect was instructed to go carefully into the cost, and on his certifying that the tender was reasonable it was accepted.

Are we to understand that this example is a fair indication of the manner in which government buildings are constructed? The original contract is let by tender for one-half the value, and the remainder given at prices arranged between the government and the contractor. Here is a building costing nearly $500,000, and the_original contract let was for only $237,-
000.	The1 extras, subsequently arranged! for with the contractor, amount to a sum equal to the original expenditure. There was no competition for about one-half the entire expenditure on the building. Is this the regular method adopted by the department ?

It is not the regular method. It depends on the circumstances and the kind of work to be done. My hon. friend, who has had a good deal to do with the erection of buildings, will realize that if the contractor is a reliable man, and will do the extra work required at a price certified to by the architect as reasonable, it is better to give him that work, as it is likely to be much better done than if there were independent contractors for the different classes of work

The minister is correct, in some respects, in saying that I have had experience in connection with firms that have had large building contracts. But we have found no difficulty, when we wanted a large building, in finding an architect who would draw in advance the plans which would cover the whole building, so that it could all be let by tender and contract, and the extras would not exceed ten per cent of the whole. In this case, you have extras practically dollar for dollar of your original contract, which, I need hardly tell the minister, is a wholly indefensible proportion.
Were the plans drawn by the architect of the department?
Yes.
Does this amount include furnishing?
Yes.
Were separate contracts given for the furnishing ?
With respect to a good deal of the furnishing, tenders were invited from the different firms.
What firms?
I cannot give them at the moment, but I will undertake to send my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) a memorandum of them.
Were tenders called for by letter or by circular, or were public advertisements issued?
By letter.
What does the bill for furnishing amount to?
In the memorandum before me there is an item for renewal of windows, lumber, hardware, furniture, &c., $40,555.04. There is also an amount due for furniture, glassware, silverware, &c., $9,000.
Was the original contract let on schedule prices?
No, it was a lump sum contract.
Then, how could it be extended ?
It was not extended.
I understood the minister to say that the work was given to the original contractor, which means, I take it, that the contract was extended.
What did the original contract include?
I wish I had the contract here.
But the minister can give it to us in a general way.
The chief architect tells me that it included the walls, the roof, the floor, the stairs and such interior walls as were, necessary to carry the roof and floors.

And were the subdividing walls, the tiling, the windows, and everything of that kind, which ordinarily goes to make a house-the plumbing and heating apparatus also-considered as extra and given out afterwards without tender or contract?

The tiling was included in the original contract. The plumbing and heating were done by the staff of the department. The subdividing walls were not included, because it could not be Mr. FOSTER.
known with accuracy how the rooms were to be divided.
Messrs. McGillivray & La-belle, the original contractors, had a contract for $237,000. How much did they receive, all told?
They received, altogether, $381,507.52.
That is, about $150,000 was paid to the contractors in addition to their original contract for work which they did under arrangement with the department?
I make it about $140,000, but my hon. friend (Mr. Ames) is substantially correct.

I think the minister will see that that method, if generally followed throughout the Public Works Department, is one open to very considerable abuse. The ordinary tenderers in competition tender with the expectation that they will have to do what their contract calls for, and that that will end the matter. If a tenderer expects to have $150,000 of extras besides, he can afford to figure low on the first estimate, in the expectation of being able to get a large margin on the balance. In that way, other tenderers competing against him who might aggregate something less, are shut out. The method is open to great abuse.

I quite agree that the method is one that ought not to be followed, and it is not followed. But this is an exceptional ease. We did not know, at least I suppose my predecessor did not know when the contract was let nor until the building was pretty well erected, what would be required. My hon. friend from North Toronto I trust is reasonably well satisfied. The chief Conservative whip of course was consulted as to the number of rooms which we required.
The Conservative whip was not consulted until everything was laid out, and then he had simply to walk through and see what was done.
Was not my hon. friend consulted last session?
After the work was all done.
It was not done last session.

The partitions were all up before I was taken into the confidence of the government at all. Then I walked through the building with the exSpeaker, and he told me what he intended to do about allotting these rooms.

I understood that last session before the partitions were finally erected, the late Speaker was consulted, and I think he consulted with the leader

of the opposition, and I think also with the the chief whip of the opposition; and it was after careful consideration that instructions were given as to the laying out of the different rooms.
The partitions were all up.
They were not all up before the late Speaker was consulted.
When was the original contract signed?

On the 9th of January,
1907.
When was the arrangement made with the contractor for additions?

From time to time as the wcrk went on and we knew what was required. I could give the dates to my hon. friend. One was on the 10th of September,
1908,	one on the 22nd of October, one on the 3rd of October, one on the 10th of April.

They amounted to $150,-
000.
What was the amount chargeable to alterations or additions in the arrangement made on April 10?

I will read the items. Taking down walls, and cement for walls, $4,990; renewals of windows, lumber, hardware and paint, $40,555.04; elevators, $17,150; alterations and improvements for ventilation, including motors, $32,516.75. That takes in the old building. Then radiators, $5,505.95; rubber tiling, $7,565.65; printing and advertising, salary of clerk of works, $3,924.87. The total expenditure up to the 31st of January was $314,038.94.
What did the extras amount to on the 10th of April?
To the difference between $314,000 and $201,830.

There does not seem to be anything in all these items which occurred gratuitously, or which could not have been foreseen, which were not in what you might call the stock parts of the work of constructing the building. Can my hon. friend point out any that were not? I do not see anything there that the late Speaker interfered with, as to what partitions should be put up, what rooms should be made, how many upon a flat, or anything of that kind. Can the minister point out anything which was done from the interference of the late Speaker, or of the whips, or of any member of parliament?

My hon. friend has misunderstood me. I did not say that the late Speaker interfered, or that the chief whip interfered. What I tried to say was that
when the original contract was let some of the plans for the laying out of the interior of the building did not appear to be feasible. The then Speaker was consulted with regard to that. I think the leader of the opposition raised a question as to the apportionment of the rooms, as to who would probably have to do with it, and it was the general opinion of the House that it should rest with the Speaker and the Minister of Public Works. We received some suggestions from the late Speaker. With regard to these items I am no table to point out any, where the suggestions of the Speaker would have changed the cost one way or the other. I am not able to say as to to what part of these works might have been provided for at the outset. Taking down the walls, that is a class of work which would ordinarily be done by the day. Then renewals of windows, lumber, hardware and paint-that was in connection with the old building, and would probably be done by the day. Then take furniture, carpets, matting, as to which prices were obtained from different trades.
Are we to understand that furniture, carpets and matting are included in the cost of the building?
In the cost which I gave.
And are charged to capital account?
That is all charged to capital account.
Does it not seem strange to charge carpets and matting that wear out in the course of a few years, to capital account?
It has been the practice, I believe, ever since confederation to charge the original furnishings of buildings at the capital, to capital account.
A bad precedent need not necessarily be followed. I think a better business method could be introduced.
When I have to do with the erection of a building under my own administration, I will carefully consider the suggestion of my hon. friend.
I want to find out how this thing happened to be constructed. Why was it constructed at all?
It was constructed with the authority and with the approval of parliament, which made an appropriation for the work two or three years ago.
Did they know what they wanted?
I presume they wanted additional accommodation.

Am I to understand from the minister that these additional works that he has mentioned were not made the subject of a specific contract and that the contractor was simply directed to go on and perform these works without any arrangement being made as to what they were to cost?

I did not say that. I said that public tenders were not called but that the contractor was invited to give a price at which he would do the work and, upon the chief architect going over the matter and certifying that the price was fair and reasonable, a contract was entered into for most of this work.
First there was a price obtained before the contractor was directed to proceed with the work.
Yes, in most cases.
Were any others asked to give figures for the same work?
No, only the contractors.
So that the prices of $150,000 worth of work were arranged between the department and contractor without competition of any kind?
That is entirely right.
Was the same plan followed with regard to the carpets and heating; that is the chief architect got prices and made arrangements with whomever he chose, no tenders being asked?

No public tenders were called. Boilers, radiators and things of that kind were purchased at market price. The chief architect has had large experience in these matters and he would know whether the contractor's price was reasonable or not. In general my hon. friend is right; no public tenders were invited, but the chief architect satisfied himself in every case that the price was fair and reasonable.

If there is open competition there is always likely to be a reduction. In this case it seems that such was not the case. Evidently the contractor had it all his own way, or, at least, in so far as he and the architect were concerned, they could fix things up to suit themselves. No outsider had any opportunity of tendering.
The minister has given the details of the work that was arranged for on April 10. How many other arrangements of that kind were made?
What was the next one?

I cannot give them in the order of date. There was one on the 10th of September, 1908, the amount being $1,011.77.
Mr. PUGSLEY
What for?
For alterations to window frames in the speaker's quarters and several other changes.
When was that arranged for?
On the 22nd of October, 1908.
What did that include?

That included certain changes in the work. They were very considerable in the Speaker's quarters, necessary by reason of the addition which was made. Certain windows were blocked up and other accommodation had to be given to the Speaker. Then there was another contract on the 3rd of October, 1908, for additional work amounting to $18,548.63.
What was included in that?
I am sorry I cannot give that to my hon. friend at present.
That is a very large one.
Yes, quite large. The chief architect tells me that is principally for division walls.
Was there a plan of the divisional walls drawn by the chief architect?
Yes.
Everything was specified?
Yes in the contract entered into.
And it was entered into without competition?
Yes. Then there was certain tile and marble work in toilet rooms and in the kitchen
What date?
I am sorry the date is omitted.
What was the amount?
This all went to the original contractors?
Yes. Then, on the 10th of April, 1908, there was a contract for a balustrade which was carried along the edge of the roof on the outside and which was necessary to give uniformity to the building.
Was not that foreseen in the original contract?
No.
What did that amount to?

$4,439.69. Of course, I am making a statement of what took place before I became minister, and the chief architect is my authority for this information. Then there was alteration to steel work and cutting floors and walls for plumbers' work and heating pipes amounting to $10,802. As to that there was no contract. Bills of cost were rendered by the contractor. The contractors have not been paid in full yet but $381,507.22 covers the original contract and also this additional work. Is there anything else you would like to have?
I did not get exactly what the furnishing cost.
I have not that separated; it is included.
There is none of it included in the items we have had?

No, but it is included in my memorandum. For lumber, hardware, furniture, carpets, glassware, &c., there is a total of $40,555.04. I can get the cost of the furniture and give it to my hon. friend later on. There is $9,000 which is due for furniture, glassware, &c. I have not given the items which make the total of $447,000 yet. I was stopped. Perhaps I had better give them now. I gave the figures of the total expenditure down to 1909 as $314,028.94. The amount due on contract, additional work, is $79,617; due on elevators, $9,150; due for heating and plumbing, $9,308; due for furniture, glassware, silverware, &c., $9,000; due for electric wiring and fixtures, $3,180; due for fitting up the Speaker's quarters, $6,000; due for painting, $5,000
What do you mean by fitting up the Speaker's quarters?
Painting, decorating, furniture, &c.
Who did the work ?
The department did some by day labour with its own staff.
Who did the chief work?
Mr. Bell, of Montreal.
How much was paid Mr. Bell?	I
He has not rendered his account yet. The chief architect tells me that the account will, including some of the furniture, be about $5,000.
Was there any contract with Mr. Bell?
No.
Was he given carte blanche?	; :j
No. He was held under strict supervision.
By whom?
By the chief architect.
In what way?
He was told to do so and so, and the prices were fixed for the different things.

Will the minister say that prices were absolutely fixed for the different parts of the work done by Mr. Bell? That there were plain and definite specifications and that Mr. Bell was instructed just what to do and not to do any more?
The chief architect tells me there was a description of the work and the price was fixed as closely as possible in work of that character.
That specification is in writing?
The chief architect tells me they have the price of practically everything in writing.
Were the arrangements for the additional work approved by the minister before the contract was closed between the architect and the contractor?

The authority was from the outset for the chief architect to make arrangements with the contractor if he would do the work at prices which he certified to be fair and reasonable. These were his general instructions. It was a departmental matter and the judgment of the chief architect in such things would prevail.
Is it the practice of the chief architect to make contracts involving such large expenditure without obtaining the approval of the minister or consulting him?
I was consulted and gave the architect authority to make this arrangement provided the prices were fair and reasonable in his judgment.
Before the arrangement was closed would the approval of the minister he asked?
I take the chief architect's certificate as to the price.
Did the government have any estimate made of what this was going to cost; did they have any idea of that as a business man would have?
When the work was undertaken the chief architect estimated that it would cost for the building-which would not include the heating or the furnishing, or this work done in the old part- $275,000.

Surely the government knew what they were going to build and must have had an estimate made. Did the architect give an estimate merely for the bare walls without any heating or lighting or any props except a few props to keep the roof up? The people of Canada should know how it is that we came to spend half a million dollars on a new wing to this building, and I want to know all details from the minister so that I may be able to tell my constituents about it. If I tell them the story I am hearing to-night they will not be satisfied.
The chief architect estimated for the walls of the building, for the principal partitions which were necessary to support the roof, and the floors, and
And the doors I suppose?
Yes, exactly, for what was included in the contract. He estimated $275,000 and the lowest tender was $237,000, or about $40,000 less. If the hon. gentleman desires I will bring down the contract.
What was his estimate for the balance of the building?

The chief architect tells me that at the time his estimate was that the partitions, and the plumbing, and the heating, and the electric lighting, and everything of that kind, would cost about $125,000 more, without the furniture.

My * recollection is that when the late Minister of Public Works decided to make the improvement he laid on the table of the House a plan, and that plan showed all the rooms as they exist now. I do not see why the tender did not cover the completed building. It was known then that heating and plumbing would have to be provided for. The contractor went on with his work, and then the Public Works Department sent their men on to undo what the contractor had done, and to put in water pipes and heating pipes. Any business man would have attended to these in the first place; but with the department they were an after consideration, and the result was to increase the cost by 50 per cent. My recollection is that the first plan included everything.
No, my hon. friend is in error.
We had the plans on the table here, and they showed the building divided into rooms.

My information is that the plans simply showed the main partitions, but not the layout of the rooms, be- * Mr. PUGSLEY.
cause I suppose the minister at that time did not know how the rooms would be divided up.
What are the partitions made of?
Terra cotta. The building, I should say, is as near fireproof as it is possible to make it.

I understood the minister to state just now that the architect had told him that the probable cost of this new wing, all completed, would be about $400,000. I wish to read to the minister and the House what the minister stated with regard to this matter last year. The estimate was:	''Parliament buildings, additions and alterations, $150,000;" and the minister said:
The note which I have from the officers of my department is that this vote of $150,000 is asked to make provision for continuing the works placed under contract in connection with the additions and alterations to the parliament buildings, which consist in extending the northwest wing northward and the residence of the Speaker of the House of Commons westward, the construction of a new upper story and roof on the tower which forms a portion of the residence, the cubic contents being 745,000 cubic feet; also for alterations to the parliament buildings in accordance with the sub-joined estimate submitted by the chief architect. The amount paid to the contractors is $76,970; renewal of windows, furniture, carpets, matting, lumber, paints, labour, $7,300.30; alterations and improvements to ventilation system, speed motor, switchboard, Nernst lamps, &c. $21,567.75; contingencies, printing, advertising and salary of clerk of works, $1,939.92, making a total expenditure up to the 31st March, 1907, of $107,777.97. Then I have further information. The amount due on the contract work is $160,463; heating and boilers, $5,000; electrical wiring and fixtures, $5,000; furniture, $10,000, &c. The total probable cost of the additions and alterations to the parliament buildings is $322,247.97.
Now, the minister told us this afternoon that the architect had assured him that the probable cost was $400,000. Which of these statements is correct, and what will be, not the probable cost, but the actual cost when the work is finished?

My hon. friend misunderstood me. I did not state that the architect had told me that the probable cost would be $400,000. He informed me that that was the estimate which he had given to the then minister. The statement that my hon. friend has read would be correct at that time, according to the progress of the work up to that date. I suppose that in the statement I gave there may not have been included certain things, such as the alteration and improvement of the ventilating system, the radiators, the elevators, the tiling and rubber tiling.

The minister's statement is this:
The total probable cost of the additions and alterations to the parliament buildings is $322,247,97.
The total cost, as I understand it, must include everything.
Did not the minister state that this $93,000 which he is asking for now is to complete the work?
Yes, the chief architect tells me that that will complete the work as outlined.
The minister said that would make the total cost of the building, including the furniture, $447,000.
Yes, and including upwards of $30,000 in connection with the old building-$447,432.90.
I would like to know if, after the contract was let, there were any alterations made in the original plans?
Nothing of any consequence.

It seems to me that, as I have listened to this discussion, there are two lessons that we may draw from it. One is as to the peculiar way in which the government carries out the principle of constructing public works by public tender and contract. Every possible rule with relation to that principle has been violated in this instance. The minister's first excuse was that there were so many complex, abstruse and unexpected things imported into this work that it was impossible to ask for tenders, and that consequently the only thing to do was to ask the contractor what he would do them for, and arrange with him to do them. But when he read the estimates, the moment he read them, we found that these added things were really stock articles, with the exception of taking down some old partitions and making some cuts between rooms, which could not be foreseen and provided for, and therefore I suppose could not be done otherwise than by day's work. With these exceptions there was nothing that could not have been put in specifications, and for which tenders could not have been asked. If there were any other things they were so very small that we might leave them out entirely in discussing the matter. Heating, electric lighting, plumbing, elevators,. all these different stock things in the construction of a building are as well defined and as easy to be estimated and put in the form of specifications as any other part of the building.
I have led my hon. friend astray. Through an unfortunate error of the typewriter, the amount as paid to the contractor is put at $381,000 instead of $281,000.
Then we have a good deal more to account for.
No, it makes the contractors paid only $281,000, and the total paid was the difference between $237,000 and $281,000.
Then my hon. friend will take back some of his arguments ?
My hon. friend will have to take back some of his criticism.

No, I have criticised on the statement of the minister. If only $45,000 to $50,000 is to be accounted for, he must account for the difference between that item of $281,000 and the $450,000, and he accounted for the difference between $381,000 and $450,000. But his statement remains that there was no competition for this difference, and that these extras were given the contractor without tender. Am I right or not?
Yes.

His second point of refuge was that there were a lot of unexpected things imported into the matter by the whips and the ex-Speaker (Mr. Sutherland). Well, the ex-Speaker shakes his head and declares he is guiltless. The whip on the Conservative side, on whom we can thoroughly rely, declares that he had nothing to do with it until he came here and found the partitions all up, and then he had to endeavour to get a little accommodation for members on the Conservative side, though the other side having pretty well taken the whole thing before he appeared on the scene.
The Conservative whip was well pleased.

So we have to eliminate certain partitions in the division of the room and that we might agree to, but they were all plain and simple, done by terra* cotta work, easily put into specifications with their dimensions, and could have been as easily put up to competition as a wall on the outside of the building. In all those cases, we have had a denegation of the principle of tender and contract, as applied to a construction which has cost the people nearly $500,000. The next lesson to be learned from this is that, under the same Minister of Public Works and the same department and staff of architects we ars going to undertake the building of great public edifices on a site which has been got at a very large expenditure. What will those cost, if this system is to be continued, which we have heard with astonishment

described by the minister, with his architect by his side, as the one under which public buildings have been constructed in the Dominion during these past years. In the Public Works Department which has been putting up buildings costing about $10,000,000, this has been the system carried on. Of that there cannot be any doubt, and there can be no doubt that this expenditure of $500,000 of the people's money does not show that value, judging from what we see in these rooms and this parliament building. No man would put $500,000 for himself into a construction which would show no more value than is shown here. Is that the way under which we are proceeding with our public works? I thought that the business of an architect was to draw plans and look after the construction, but the minister says that he is practically the man who arranged the terms upon which these things are done. I do not think that that is any part of the architect's branch. It is unwise and unfortunate that the architect's branch should be mixed up in the least with a department of the government which has to see what prices are to be paid and what amount of money expended. An architect is for the purpose of advising and having the specifications properly drawn and the plans properly made and putting information into the hands of the proper officers to call for tenders and award them. The advice of an architect is always good in these matters, but I do not think he should have been put in the position of making the best terms with the contractor. Here you have an original contract for $237,000 and a building when constructed costing $500,000, and practically the contractor has had, without competition, every bit of extra work at his own prices. Anybody knows, who has read the proceedings of the Cassels' Commission, that an officer of the department has no show for his life when there is a question between a contractor and the minister. The officer is used as the buffer, but the contractor gets about what he wants, and the architect and the officers who stand in between the two ought not to be! placed in the position of the responsible minister who has to see what prices should be paid. That, however, has been the case during this transaction. Will the minister tell this House what we have to show for that $500,000 of the people's money?

I admire some of the qualities of my hon. friend and often wonder at the vast amount of information which he possesses. But as regards the construction of a building, he is deplorably ignorant. He says that, with regard to the prices for these different works, I should not have relied on the architect at all, but have fixed the prices myself. I venture to say there is no private individual who has ever erected a building, in connection with which he Mr. FOSTER.
has had, during the progress of the work to do certain things not specified in the contract. It is the architect who makes out the estimates and specifications at the outset and fixes the prices. Why? Because his knowledge and experience enable him to form a judgment as to what are fair prices, and all contracts provide that if payments are made from time to time they are to be made on progress estimates certified to by the architect. It is the architect on whom the owner places reliance ; and I can well understand that if a minister had made certain payments to the contractor, without having the information from the architect as to what that work is worth, my hon. friend would have justly _ complained that the minister had no business to do that but should have relied on his architect.
Now, he has made the suggestion that the Cassels' inquiry has shown that the officials of the department have no independence, that they cannot exercise an honest judgment, but are obliged to do whatever the minister wishes them to do. He must know something of the character, reputation and standing of the chief architect of 'the; Department of Public Works. That gentleman was appointed in 1871, some thirty-eight years ago, and I would not like to be the minister who would ask the chief architect to vary his figures by one iota to satisfy me or any other member of the government. While I have been minister-and no doubt, the same remark would apply to my predecessor, both of this government and of previous governments-the judgment of the present chief architect could be relied upon with a great deal of confidence. At all events, he is a man who will exercise his own independent judgment, and will not be influenced by any minister under whom he might serve. I have already called attention to an unfortunate error in the figures furnished me which caused me to overstate the amount actually paid to the contractors by about $100,000.
