That makes the total amount of additional work, including these partitions, about $44,000 instead of $150,000 as I unwittingly led by my hon. friend from St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) to believe. I am sure that, looking over these figures, the hon. gentleman will see that, in view of

the class of work to be done and the difficulty which, apparently, the former minister, Mr. Hyman, had in determining what partitions were to be erected, and determining how the rooms were to be laid out, it was not unreasonable that the work should be done upon prices given by the contractor. And he will see that it could not be done by a separate contract that might be given to an outsider, because, in that case, the work of the two contractors would be likely to clash. The important question is whether the chief architect could be relied upon to determine what were fair and reasonable prices.
Then how does the minister explain the increase of $169,000 over the $281,000?
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster) will find that the figures I have given do not alter the total previously given, $447,732.

If the minister will pardon me a moment, there is one matter of detail to which I would like to call attention. The room which has been allotted to the Conservative members is supposed to have upper double windows. If the minister will step around to that room, if he cannot give the architect a suggestion, I shall be surprised. The windows should be on hinges; bolted, they are no use.
The chief architect will make a note of that point.
The building will cost $447,000?	.

Including the furniture. I understand my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) to ask, ' What have you to show for it ? ' One has only to go through the building, including the upper stories, and to view the magnificent restaurant and the different rooms set apart for the accommodation, and I think any one of experience will say that we have received good value for our money.

It seems from what we have been able to ascertain from the minister that there is a difference of nearly $100,000 between the estimated cost of the building as made by the architect, and the actual cost. This is a very large difference. I understood the minister to say in answer to my hon. friend from North Toronto, that the architect was the man that did everything. But does any man in this country putting up a building allow the architect to make whatever arrangements he likes with the contractor? The man who furnishes the money does not allow the architect to go to the contractor and say he may do just as he likes. Of course, everybody knows that we must rely a good deal upon the architect, but not to the extent
that has been done in this case. I am satisfied to spend a good deal of money in Ottawa, but I do not want to see all the money of the Dominion of Canada spent here; I want some of it spent in other parts of the country.
Can the minister say what amount of space or what number of rooms provided by this expenditure, has gone to the accommodation of officers of the House?
That has all appeared in the 'Hansard,' to which I would refer my hon. friend.

I think the officials have more space than the members. I want to say in connection with the allotment of rooms to the opposition, that just before the prorogation of parliament last year the late Speaker invited the chief government whip (Mr. Calvert) and myself to go through the building, and he gave us what his plan was at that time, giving comfortable quarters to the leader of the opposition in old No. 6, also where he proposed making the Premier's room,~ and then a room for the whips. His plan was to give a certain proportion to the government side and a certain proportion to the opposition side. But that arrangement was not carried out. When I came down here after the allotment was made, I found that the plans of the late Speaker concerning a room for the opposition leader and the Conservative whips had been carried out. Then after some negotiations, we secured quarters for the balance of our contingent in the rooms that had been occupied previously by members supporting the government. According to the returns brought down, I think we got our fair share of the space, but we have not got our fair share of the new quarters.

In what I had to do with the matter I tried to make it as convenient as possible for our hon. friends opposite. There is some dissatisfaction among them, and there is dissatisfaction among our own friends, who feel they have not got the accommodation they would like. Even a minister of the Crown came to me not long ago and complained. But we tried to satisfy everybody who had claims for accommodation.

An arvnlication is in and I hope it will be carried out soon, to give us Conservative members, better seating accommodation. We have a lot of old dilapidated chairs there which ought to be stored. When we had a caucus this morning we had to send into the room of the Minister of Finance to get chairs.
The chairs have been ordered.
It is a notorious fact that officials of this House are better provided for than the members, so much so that some of the officials are renting rooms.
What official is renting rooms?
Right downstairs there.
I shall be glad to deal with that matter when my attention is called to it.
I know that was the state of affairs formerly.

I think it must have been some time ago.
Ottawa Royal Mint, refinery, $30,000.

I have put in this item at the request of the Minister of Finance, who says it is urgently needed. The building is expected to cost $30,000. Nothing has been done yet. It is intended to erect a building 35 x 60 feet, one story high, on stone foundations, fireproof throughout, and with strong vaults.
Will this include the refining machinery?
Only the building.
Is the minister prepared to state what the plant will cost?
That is a matter for the Finance Department rather than mine, for the officers of the mint.
What will this make the total cost?
The total expenditure to the 31st of December last was $520,233.88. That includes the site for the building, the wiring, the machinery, tools and everything.
How much did the fence cost?

We heard so much about that last session that I hoped my hon. friend would not refer to it again. But my hon. friend forgets about the guard-rooms, there are very substantial guard-rooms embraced in the cost.
What size?
Go down and look at them. The total amount for this high iron fence, with the granite foundations and guard-rooms, was $43,529.
When are the members going to be taken through the mint?
Any time they wish, when an arrangement can be made.
Were tenders called for?
No public tenders, it was done by contract.
How was the arrangement arrived at by which the contractors charged that expenditure of $43,529 ?

Plans were prepared for the work to be done and a tender was asked Mr. BARR.
from the contractor. He submitted a tender which the chief architect thought to be fair and reasonable, and upon his certificate the contract was let.
So that no one else was given the opportunity to compete for the work although plans were prepared beforehand?
There were no public tenders called.

This is in no way a part of the building itself. There was no reason why the work of erecting a fence and inclosing the property could not have been put up to public tender and contract. What possible reason was there why this work was not thrown open to competition?

This was all arranged for before I became minister, but I am informed that the contractor had all his plant there, encumbering the ground, and it was thought inconvenient to bring in another contractor. The Master of the Mint was pressing for the erection these guard houses, and it had to be done as quickly as possible because they would not open the mint until these things were provided, and that is the reason why it was not put up to public competition.
Has anybody ever got over that fence?
It is pretty difficult; he would have to be quite a jumper.
Was there one contract for the fence and the guard house?
One contract.
The question was asked a session or two ago and the statement was made that the fence cost $29,000 and the guard house $13,000 or $14,000.
It was one contract.
Was not the price fixed separately for the guard-house?
No, it was one price.

In this work we have a repetition of what we had in the other case. While the contractors, Messrs. Sullivan & Langdon, have a contract calling for $263,000, the total payment to them is $325,000, so that we have these contractors receiving $60,000 over their contract price without any tenders being asked or without any opportunity for competition on the part of others. That is the same thing repeated in connection with the Mint that we have in connection with this addition to the parliament buildings.
That is something I would not justify unless there were very special reasons for it, and in this case there were special reasons.
There are always special reasons.

It apparently was not anticipated that a fence and guard-room of this character were required. It had been announced that the Mint would open at a certain time and the Imperial authorities required that the fence and the guardhouses should be built before they would allow the Mint to be opened. It was work which was very urgent, and it was deemed very much better to allow this contractor, who was a most reliable contractor, to do the work at what the chief architect thought was a fair and reasonable price.
Is it not a fact that the law states that the Minister of Public Works shall not expend any amount over $5,000 without calling for tenders?
Yes, but there is an exception to the law. The law provides that he cannot do it except in cases of emergency.
Oh, oh.
This was a case of that kind.
I would like to ask the minister where there is any condition about an emergency in the statute? I think not.
Yes, it is in the statute.
The statute provides that an order in council, signed by His Excellency and setting forth the emergency, shall be passed.
I am quite aware of the fact, and in this case the grounds of the emergency were set out and the order m council passed.
Was there an order in council passed in each of the cases in reference to this new wing in which work was given without contract or tender amounting to more than $5,000.
Yes, as to the elevators, which I think is the only one that is over $5,000.
No.
Yes.
There is one of $10,800 and another of $18,000.
I cannot tell as to other amounts over $5,000, but I know that in the case of the elevators that was done.
The minister would not violate the law ?
He would not intentionally.
Did he not know what the law was?
Yes.
And it has been violated?
My practice has always been in every case where it is over $5,000 to have an order in council setting forth the grounds of emergency.
Will the minister see if in these three cases there was an order in council?
Yes.
Will the minister bring down the order in council because it certainly will be a curiosity to place before the House.
For the guard-house and fence? I will be glad to.
And then afterwards we may take a vote to send it down to the archives.
I would like to ask the minister if the plan which has been prepared for the refinery provides for the complete building or just for the walls?
This estimate is for the complete building, but not for the refining plant.

I understood the minister to say that the emergency arose out of the fact that the Imperial government insisted that this guard-house and fence should be built before the Mint was opened. I would ask the minister if the Mint was not opened before the guard-house and fence were constructed? The guard-house was not finished before we went away from here last year.
My information was that the fence was completed.
The fence was, but not the guard-room.
Perhaps my remarks should be limited to the fence.
Then you broke the law with regard to the guard-room?
Possibly they are separate.	.

I would ask the minister to bring down all the orders in council or all the amounts that have been expended over and above $5,000 without tender and contract upon the new wing as well as upon the building under discussion.

I stated to the committee that I thought there was one providing for the purchase of the elevators from the Otis-Fensom Company, but I was not sure whether there were any others. If there are I will bring them down.

If there were not, the expenditures would be contrary to law.
Ottawa, Victoria Memorial Museum, $400,-
000.

Many hon. gentlemen are familiar with this building. The vote is $400,000 and this is to continue the erection of the Victoria Memorial Museum. The chief architect estimated this building would cost $1,250,000 but the actual contract is only $950,000. It was let to Mr. Goodwin who is a very experienced contractor at some $300,000 less than the chief architect estimated. The contractor has gone ahead very satisfactorily with his work and I am much afraid he will not make much out of it.
How much has been expended up to the present?
Altogether, up to the 28th of December, $786,056.73 including $75,000 cost of site.
How much is required to complete?
Including the site, furniture, fittings, elevators, &c., it is supposed that the total cost to complete and equip will be $1,312,143.15.
When do you expect it will be completed?
In fifteen months oi eighteen months.
Are you asking for this $400,000, expecting that it will completely finish the work?
We expect it will cost $100,000 more.
How much do you consider the building will have cost at the end of the present fiscal year?
The actual expenditure will be about $812,000.
Then you only expect to spend $26,000, for the remainder of the fiscal year?

Yes. Perhaps I had better give the figures: Paid for site $75,000; incidental expenses, surveying, printing, advertising, clerk of works salary, &c., $13,306.73; laying of drain $4,500; paid to the contractor up to the 28th of December, $693,250; total expenditure to 28th of December, $786,056.73; amount due on contract work when contract is finished, $256,750; heating apparatus, boilers, &c., (es-Mr. CROSBY.	i	 i
timated) $50,000; electric wiring, fixtures, (estimated) $25,000; elevators (estimated) $40,000; fittings, furniture (estimated) $100, 000; carving (estimated) $15,000; superintendence, &c. (estimated) $29,000. That makes the total including, site, furnishing, fittings, &e., $1,312,143.15.
Is any of the money at present voted to go to other portions of the work that are not included in the contract of George Goodwin?
Yes.
Will the minister give us his assurance that there will be proper competition, and opportunity given to other people besides Mr. Goodwin to tender in connection with this work?

No, I would not like to give my hon. friend that assurance and I will tell you why: Mr. George Goodwin is as reliable a contractor as there is in Canada. He has taken this contract at about $300,000 less than the chief architect's estimate.
Did he build the Laurier tower which fell down?

I do not know as to that. Mr. Goodwin is a splendid contractor and everybody will say that he has done a thoroughly good job on that museum. His tender was I think $275,000 less than the next lowest tender, but Mr. Goodwin is a man who is prepared to carry out what he undertakes. Now, my own view would be that there are advantages, in the case of a building like that, in having the contractor do the heating, and plumbing, and work of that character, and if Mr. Goodwin is prepared to do that work at a figure which the chief architect is prepared to say is fair and reasonable I will say frankly, that I would be disposed, if it can be done, to give that work to Mr. George Goodwin, the contractor. I do not say it will be done but I am not prepared now to give my hon. friend the assurance that it will not be done.

Here we have a distinct avowal in advance that once a contractor is in possession of the four walls and the roof of a building he practically has the absolute refusal of all the remaining work. He can do it without tender and by a simple arrangement between himself and the architect. That is just the way to pay the highest possible price for the additional work required on the building. If that is the fixed policy of the department we must expect to pay very high prices and oftentimes in excess of the real value of the work. That is not the way public establishments do their business, at least such as I have had to do with. Further, it is not fair to other contractors if it is

understood that if a contractor secures a contract even at a low figure he will have an opportunity of making very large returns upon his extras. If the government is favourable to the contractor he is given the opportunity to continue the extra work at a price to be arranged between himself and the architect and if the government is not favourable to him he is deprived of that chance to make money.

As a general proposition the contracts for all work on a building should be let by public tender and I have asked the architect in future, as far as possible, to let the contract in the first place including heating, and wiring, and all these things so far as that can be done.
That is fair.

But here is a very large and expensive building, one which has been built with great care and in the most satisfactory way by the contractor. As he is rushing along his work towards completion, it might cause great dissatisfaction to put in three or four sub-contractors, each acting independently and under no one control. Therefore, if I can be assured by the chief architect that Mr. Goodwin is prepared to do this work at a fair and reasonable price, I would have no hesitation myself in recommending His Excellency in Council to give the work to the contractor.

If I take the architect's estimate of the cost of this building, $1,250,000, and then take the contract price at which we are getting it built, $950,000, does it not mean that the architect is very extravagant in his estimates ?
Take the next tender.

I am speaking of the estimate of the architect. I do not want to say anything against him, but it strikes me that it is not safe to allow him to name the price of anything that goes into that building.

We have had some experience in the past of architects and engineers certifying that prices are fair and reasonable. I could give a number of instances, but I need only mention the lighting of the Cornwall canal. When a dispute arose between the Auditor General and the party who was paid for the service, the account was cut down from $52,000 to $29,000, because the Auditor General would not agree to it, even though the engineer had certified that the price was fair and reasonable, and recommended the payment of the money and the Minister of Railways and Canals had assented ; and then the Auditor General declared that it was $10,000 too high still. We have brought a great many instances of this kind to light during the last few years. Is it any wonder that we
should be a little suspicious in passing this matter over to the tender mercies of any;
architect ?
At six o'clock, committee took recess.
After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock.
If I understood the minister aright, the contract for this building covers only the building proper, and other arrangements will have to be made for the fittings.
In the case of the Victoria Museum, the contract did not include heating apparatus, electric wiring, elevators, fittings and furniture and carving.
I also understood that it was the intention of the minister to give the contract for these works to the gentleman who had the contract for the building.
I said I was not prepared to give an assurance that that would not be done.
We gathered from the debate that that would probably take place.
Possibly.

If that principle were generally accepted, a contractor could wetl take his contracts at a much reduced rate, with the expectation and strong probabilities of making good out of these later contracts. I presume that the heating, wiring, and so on will cost $100,000, and probably more?
The estimate is $85,000.

Then, it is not difficult to believe that they will cost $100,000. This is a principle to which I very much object-that a contract should be made for so large a building as this, with what looks like a full intention of giving the contracts for the fittings to the same party without tender. I do not think that is a businesslike way or one that will satisfy the people. I do not see why others should not have the opportunity of tendering if they desire to do so.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Schaffner) understood me correctly that I would not give assurance that this would not be done. And my present view would be that, if the contractor is willing to undertake the work at a price that the chief architect, in whose judgment I have the greatest possible confidence, certified to be fair and reasonable, I would be disposed to recommend to my colleagues, under the circumstances, that the present contractor should have the contract. My first

reason is because of the low figure at which he undertook the work of the building, and because I am satisfied that he has lost money, his tender being $300,000 below the estimate of the chief architect, and $275,000 lower than that of the next lowest tenderer. Another reason is the very satisfactory way in which he has done the work. Another reason is that it would be much more satisfactory to have the work go on under one contractor than under a separate contractor.

That may all be very true, but it is not a very good reason for the course which the minister suggests. The mere fact that the contractor has taken the contract at what is supposed to be too low a figure and has lost money is not sufficient reason for taking this particular means of making that money up to him.
Can't very well make up $300,000 on a contract for $85,000.
If the trimmings cost as much more than the estimate as the building has done-
This building is costing much less than the estimate. The architect's estimate was $1,250,000 and the contract is $950,000.
It is not finished yet.
This was the estimate of only that part which was contracted for. It did not include the heating apparatus, the electric wiring, elevators, fittings and furniture and carving.
And, if I understood the minister correctly, he wants to throw $200,000 or $300,000 to this contractor, whoever he may be, because he took the contract at too low a figure-
I am sure my hon. friend (Mr. Crosby) does not wish to misunderstand me. The total estimate for these fittings is $85,000. I certainly am not throwing $300,000 to him.

The minister's anxiety concerning the contractor arises from the fact that the contractor is supposed to be losing money by this contract. There is just as much reason for us to conclude that the architect was out in his estimate. The very fact that he estimated $1,250,000 for the construction of a building, and that a contractor whom the minister describes as one of the best contractors in the Dominion offers to construct that building for $950,000 is strong reason why this committee should not accept him as the final authority in these matters when he is so extravagant in his estimates. I, for one, am not going to sit in this House and vote in favour of contracts being given in this Mr. PUGSLEY.
way. Unless there is some indication that this work is going to be let by tender and contract, I shall not agree to such a vote without registering my strong protest against dealing with the public money in this manner.

When we were discussing the last item, the minister said, as I understood him, that it was an exceptional case, but that if he had had control from the beginning, he would not have let the contract in the way in which it was let. But now, when we come to consider this item, the minister acknowledges that he is going to do exactly the same thing as his predecessor did; that is, notwithstanding that the original contract was let after tenders called, he intends to give the contract for the remaining portion of the work to the person who has received the contract and without calling for further tenders. This completely justifies the complaint that the opposition is making against a contract of this kind. Once a party tendering knows that when he gets a contract for a certain portion, he will get a contract for the balance of the works without tender that eliminates the principle of competition. It puts the other parties who tender, and who do not know that the one whose tender would be accepted was bound to get the balance of the work without competition, at a disadvantage; and it enables the one who knew this, to tender at a lower figure than he otherwise would, relying on increased profits in the additional work which he would secure without tender, so that in reality he is not the lowest tenderer. Whenever a vote is asked for an appropriation, the minister should be in a position to let us know what the work will cost altogether and call for tenders for the entire work, so that all who tender may be on an equal footing. It is not fair to the country to let a portion of the contract by tender and then give the balance without competition to favoured friends of the government. The minister tells us that the reason why he grants the remainder of the contract to the one whose tender is accepted is because his tender was the cheapest, but the reason why this man tendered at the lowest figures may have been because he knew that the minister was going to do what he has told us tonight he intended doing.
Who is the clerk of works?
Mr. B. Cantlie.-
Has he had any experience in supervising the construction of public buildings?
About ten years.
Is he the gentleman who was the clerk of works on the Laurier tower?
No.

I do not think it is possible to have a more vicious system than that which the minister has just explained to us. We know what it has led to in the department which has been under investigation and which is the only one in which there was a little lift of the curtain. This system of giving contracts for part of the work to one man, after inviting public tenders, and then giving him the balance without tender, is bound to result in great loss to the country and public scandal. I do not think we can condemn it in sufficiently strong terms, and I hope the minister will see his way to giving us the strongest assurance that no such method will be followed by the government in the future. I would ask him whether his architect has an absolutely free hand in giving the extras to whom he likes, or whether he must give them to those who are on the patronage list?

The patronage list has been abolished in my department and there is no question of patronage here. It is simply a question as to -whether public tenders shall be invited for the fittings, or *whether an arrangement be made with the contractor, provided he is willing to do the work at a price which our chief architect considers fair and reasonable. Some little time ago, after I became minister-and it has been impressed on my attention more recently because of the consideration I have givfen in this building and one or two others-I came to the conclusion that it is desirable, as far as possible, to provide in the original contract for all the different classes* of work. I quite agree with the hon. gentleman who has just spoken that it is better to do that, and that is my intention. As far as possible, in letting contracts in future, I intend that the original contract shall provide for everything which can be reasonably foreseen.
Why not do it now?

I cannot do it in this case because the building is nearly completed. Here is a very expensive building which, although not completed, is pretty well on to completion, and the wiring and heating ought to be going on simultaneously with the finishing up of the work. Mv experience is that if we have an honest contractor and can fix a reasonable price with him, it is infinitely better for him to do the work than have two or three sub-contractors whose men will be quarrelling together as to how the work will go along.
Was the contract let without reservation on the part of the government that they could let other workmen into the building?
Of course we can.

Better delay the completion
of the building for six months and let us have an honest tender for the work not under contract and remaining to be done, and not have the very grave suspicion aroused which a system of this sort is bound to excite.
1 do not think anybody can have any suspicion.
I am going to vote against this item unless we have some assurance from the minister that the work, not let by contract and yet to be done, will he open to public competition.
I shall be very sorry if the hon. gentleman votes against it.
There will be a time when the minister will have reason to be sorry.
What are the duties of a clerk of works ?
He has to be on the spot constantly and see that the contractor carries out the plans and specifications and also the instructions and the directions of the architect.

It seems to me that a man who will work for $3.50 per day is hardly capable of doing that work. When you let a contract involving a million dollars and then hire a man at $3.50 per day to pass on the technical work and stand between the contractor and the government, I should say that a man who will work for that wage is not capable of fulfilling these duties. If he were, he would command higher pay.
We have an experienced architect on our staff who is there constantly in addition to the clerk of works.

In that case the clerk of works is not required at all. Either he is capable of overseeing the work or he is not. If he is, you do not require an architect there with him; and if he is not, he is no use there at all.
Amherst, public buildings, Nova Scotia- improvements, $2,000.

This is to make provision for the purchase of a tower clock and its installation and also for the re-wiring of the entire building. I may say that at the last session of parliament there was voted $2,500 for this purpose; of that amount $809 was available on the 1st of February.
How big does the town have to be before it gets a town clock?

Some cases have been brought to my notice where towers have been erected on the various buildings intended for a clock; in some cases towers



were erected ten or fifteen years ago for the purpose of a clock. In the case of Amherst, my attention was called to the fact that the building had an unfinished appearance, was unsightly, and I gave directions to have a clock put in the tower.

I would ask the minister whether his attention has been drawn to a "fact that quite xecently a judgment was given in England against a man who had put up a public clock. As time went on the clock was neglected, it was not wound up, and some citizens sued the man, and I think got damages for misleading them as to the time of day. It was held that a public body who erected a town clock for the public good was bound to keep the clock in order. Now the minister sees the posi-bility that the government may be sued if it neglects to keep these town clocks in proper order.

We will take the chances of that.
Bridgewater, public buildings, $6,000.

This is to make provision for continuing during the coming years the construction of a public building in the town of Bridgewater. It is to be two stories, on a stone foundation, and intended to provide accommodation for post office, customs house, etc. The total amount of the contract is $23,500.
How much has been already expended on the contract?
There has been paid to the contractor already $23,710. There has been some extra work.

After having paid the contractor the full amount of his contract, why do you want this $6,000 more?
. Mr. PUGSLEY. The explanation of that is that subsequently to the contract being awarded it was decided to put a clock in this building, and to erect a tower for the purpose; consequently the contract was changed, and it was agreed to pay the contractors for that $2,882.

Where is the rest of the
$0,000?

I will give the whole statement. Amount paid for site, $5,500; for legal expenses, survey of site, printing, advertising and clerk of works, $1,042.62. There was paid on account for heating apparatus and for boiler, $594, and there is still due for heating apparatus, $656. Due on electric wiring and fixtures, $1,000; fittings, furniture, lock boxes, the estimate is $4,000; sidewalks and fences, $1,000; contingencies of various, kinds, $2,000. The total estimated cost, with the site of the building, heating, electric wiring and fixtures, $14,539.80. The total expenditure to the 31st of December was $30,846.80. Assumed Mr. PUGSLEY.
expenditure from 31st December last to 31st March, $2,692. The population of Bridgewater is nearly 3,000.

Is it the intention of the minister to put a clock in every public building where there is a tower constructed for that purpose?
( Mr. PUGSLEY. There is no settled policy. I have put clocks in several public buildings where it has been represented to me that they were desirable. But I cannot say that I will do it in every public building.

The minister gave as a reason for putting a clock in the public building at Amherst that there was a tower erected for the purpose, and it was unsightly without a clock. But in this case he seems to have decided to erect a public building without a tower, and afterwards changed his mind. Now when did he reach the conclusion that it was wise, after the contract was let, to change the plans and specifications and erect a tower and put in a clock?

That was decided along in the spring of 1908. I may say that by reason of the location of the building at Bridgewater, it was strongly represented to me that a tower and clock would greatly improve the appearance of the building, and as the expense would not be great I yielded to the representations. I have plenty of precedents for that. When our friends opposite were in power many public buildings were erected in some of which clocks were placed, and others were left unsightly without clocks.

I have a distinct recollection that the principle of supplying clocks was strongly condemned by the hon. gentleman's friends when in opposition. It was declared to be extravagant, wrong and unjustifiable. Now the hon. gentleman, supported by his friends, comes forward and does the very thing which they so strongly condemned. Two wrongs can never make a right. If it was wrong for the hon. gentleman's predecessors to do it surely there is no justification for him repeating that wrong because, from his intelligence, he must have known better.
You would say that it was right then.

In explanation of the purpose of putting a tower on this building, I may say that the building belongs to a new design introduced by the Department of Public Works about a year ago. It is a flat-roofed building. The appearance of the building is rather low and there were very strong representations made on behalf of the people of the town to alter the exterior appearance of the building by placing a tower upon it, or by mak-

ing some other change. It did add a little to the cost, but I may say that if any hon. gentleman saw the building he would feel that the department was strictly justified in putting on this tower.
How much did the tower and clock cost?
The tower cost $2,882 and the clock will probably cost $1,500 or $2,000.
Is this a post office building?
Post office and customs house.
Have the government any settled policy as to where buildings of that description should be erected, having reference to population?

No rule has been laid down as to the exact number of people required in a place in order to justify the erection therein of a public building. Population does not always govern. Something may depend upon the trade that is done in a place, upon the customs receipts, upon the existing post office accommodation, upon the possibility or otherwise of renting suitable buildings for public purposes and sometimes upon whether it is a county town or not. There has been one rule laid down, not as a fixed rule, but it has been recognized and, I think, it was so stated by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), and that is that this government will be disposed to favour as rapidly as might reasonably be done, the erection of one public building in a county, that public building to be in the county town. But, of course, it can be seen that that rule cannot always be adhered to, because it sometimes happens that the county town may not be the most important town in the county.
You think there should be one in every county?
I think that should be the ultimate aim to which we should look forward.
Is Bridgewater a county town?
I do not think it is.

It is and it is not. There are two towns in the county of Lunenburg, each of which regards itself as a county town because each is the seat of courts. It is rather an important town, and I do not think that any gentleman can make any valid objection to this expenditure.
What is the population?
About 2,000.
What is the post office revenue?
It was not large enough to be incorporated when the census was taken.
The post office revenue is $5,590, the customs duties, $4,448; money orders issued, $59,000, and money orders paid, $21,000.

I just came in a few moments ago and I understood that the discussion was centring on public buildings in county towns. I desire to draw the attention of the hon. gentleman to the fact that there is a county town in the county which I have the honour to represent and during the recent election campaign my opponent gave a very strong promise that a post office would be erected in the town of Milton, the county town. He gave a very strong assurance of what he would accomplish when he came here. Unfortunately for the people who wanted a post office, he did not come, but I trust it may not be so unfortunate after all, because I believe that if the Minister of Public Works made the promise that he would erect a post office in that town he would not hesitate to do it even if the gentleman who conveyed that promise to the people should not have been elected.
What is the population?
The population, I presume, is 1,700 or 1,800.
Do you favour erecting one there?

Certainly, I would favour the erection of a post office in Milton. We had the strong assurance of the government candidate during the election that a post office would be erected in that town. I can hardly assume that my opponent made that promise without having had some guarantee from the minister that the promise would be implemented, and I do not think the minister would go so far as to give that assurance only on the condition that my opponent would be elected. I believe he is too honourable. I think that if he gave the promise at all it should ' be implemented no matter who was elected. All I ask is that the promise may be implemented by the erection of a public building in Milton. We have no public building in the county of Halton. There are some five towns and villages about the same size as Milton, not one of which has a public building, and I do not think I am asking too much when I ask the minister to carry out the pledge which was given by my opponent to the people of Milton that a post office should be erected there in the event of his return. I would like the minister to say whether he made

that promise and, if so, is it his intention to carry it out and give us a public building during the current year ?

I may say to my hon. friend that I do not call to my mind at the present moment whether I was communicated with on the subject of a public building or not. I do remember my hon. friend presenting, at the last session of this parliament, the claims of Milton so strongly that I am inclined to think that he almost persuaded me that Milton should have a public building, but I can say to my hon. friend, and it may do for the whole of this discussion in regard to public buildings, that he will not find that I have ever, since I have been Minister of Public Works, made a promise, or authorized anybody else to make a promise for the erection of a public building conditional upon the election of a supporter of the government. Wherever I have made a statement that a public building will be erected it is an unqualified statement. If I have made any promise with regard to Milton or with regard to any other public building it will be carried out at the very earliest opportunity. I can tell my hon. friend that so far as I remember there are no amounts in the estimates this year for public buildings other than those in respect of which tenders have already been called. In view of the state of the revenue we have felt obliged to postpone for another year the erection of a great many public buildings for which appropriations were made last session and which we have not felt in a position to go on with at the present time. I am afraid that the public building at Milton, if one is to be erected there, would have to stand over the same as the rest.
There has been a discussion as to the erection of a town clock; may I ask the minister if he intends to put a clock in the Conservative members' room?
Considering the youth and character of my hon. friend (Mr. Henderson) I think we should put a ' watch ' there.
What will be the total cost of the Bridgewater building?

Including everything to complete, it is estimated to cost $42,539.80.
Glace Bay, public buildings, $12,000.

This is to complete this building providing accommodation for post office, custom house, inland revenue, examining warehouse, weights and measures. The total cost including the site, heating, electric wiring, &c., is estimated at $54,859.85.
What is the population of Glace Bay?
7,000 by census of 1901. I am informed it is probably 15,000 now.
What is the estimated cost of this building?
What was the contract price and how much has been expended to date?
The contract price $24,000; expended to 31st of December, $41,540 which includes $11,599 for the site.
Will this vote complete the building?
We expect it will.
Will this building have a tower and clock?
No.

It would appear to me that the necessity for erecting towers on these public buildings and providing them with clocks becomes very pressing on the eve of an election. For instance, there was no clock on the Sydney building for a great many years, but on the eve of the 1904 election a stipendiary magistrate Mr. A. G. Maclean and a jeweller by the name of Fred. Lighter were appointed a committee to go to the old country to select a clock. The jeweller might have been a very good man for the purpose but I doubt the qualifications of the stipendiary magistrate; anyhow the clock has never given satisfaction. I suggest with all deference to the minister that instead of providing these buildings with towers which in the case of Amherst cost $2,800, and clocks which cost from $1,500 to $3,000, it would be much better to dispense with these luxuries which are much like the fifth wheel on a carriage, and to apply the money to the Postmaster General's Department towards giving a better mail service to the people in the scattered districts of Nova Scotia.
Guysborough public buildings, improvements, $1,200.
This is to complete the installation of a clock and to provide an acetylene gas plant.
What is the population of Guysborough?
About 1,500 last census.
What will these improvements cost?

About $2,000.
Halifax. Dominion building, improvements, repairs, etc., $75,000.

This vote is for the purpose of remodelling the whole interior of the Halifax Dominion building, making it

fire proof and fitting it for post office purposes and assistant receiver general's offices The customs, examining warehouse and inland revenue offices have been removed to the new customs building, and it is found necessary to remodel this building to fit it for post office purposes.
It is being done by contract.
Yes.
Who has the contract?
Mr. Keefe.
Will this vote complete?
No, it will require $70,000 more. The total probable cost including everything is $165,000.
Is the contract let for $165,000?

No, the contract, including the wiring, is let for $94,000. In addition, the heating and boilers, it is estimated, will cost $15,000, electric fixtures $1,500, fittings, furniture and lock boxes $25,000, vault lining of doors $10,000, contingencies and superintendence $19,500; total estimated cost $165,000.
Is this remodelling an old building?
Yes.
When is this building to be completed?
On the 18th of March, 1910.
Was the contract let by public tender?
Yes.
Who are the contractors?
Mr. Keefe, of Halifax.
What is the amount of his tender?
$94,000. The other tenderers were for $114,000 and $145,000 respectively.
How much is the total work to cost, all completed?
Is it the intention of the minister to let the difference between the contract and the total cost, amounting to $70,000, by tender or to the present contractor?
My intention is to let that by tender, as far as we can do so.
How does the minister propose to let this addition of $70,000 by tender and not the addition for the museum?

I have endeavoured to explain that there are special conditions with respect to the museum which do not exist with respect to this building. At all events, I do not know any special reason why we should not ask for tenders for this work, as we have ample time to do it.

I fail to see what the special conditions are. The minister has given us no special logical reason why he should not let the remainder of the museum work by tender. In the construction of all large buildings there are many contractors for different trades working at the same time.
Does the hon. gentleman object to my letting this by tender?
No, but I am asking why the minister has not done it in the case of the museum.
We are now discussing the Halifax public building.

I am asking the minister if he can give me any special reason why he adopts the principle of letting the remainder of this work by tender when he does not adopt that principle in the case of the museum.
I have already answered. The hon. gentleman will find it all in 'Hansard.'
Is there provision in this contract for other contractors to occupy the building at the same time, in the event of letting other portions of the work to other contractors?

Yes.
Halifax-Immigrant Detention Building-Hospital, $2,500.

This is a revote. It is to provide for the erection of a stable in the immigration detention grounds at Halifax. It has been requested by the Superintendent of Immigration, and the estimated cost is $2,500.
Does that complete the entire outfit at the Halifax immigration detention building?

Yes.
New Glasgow public building-improvements, $1,000.
I would like to ask the hon. Minister of Public Works what the nature of these improvements is and at whose request they are made?

This amount is for some alterations to be made in the building, and also for the purchase of a clock to be placed in the tower. The chief architect tells me that the Customs Department have applied for these changes.
From whom does the government purchase these Nova Scotia clocks?
Most of them are obtained in the old country; none of them are made in Canada.
How many public buildings in Nova Scotia have been supplied with clocks? I think the hon. minister is showing partiality to Nova Scotia. Only one was promised in Ontario-that was in Berlin.

Is the hon. Minister of Public Works aware that the 'Eastern Chronicle,' published in New Glasgow, and the organ of this government in East Pictou, last month commented editorially on this expense, pointing out that it was altogether unnecessary and uncalled for, and that, as the editor had seen the alterations, they were calculated to weaken the building by the cutting of rafters and beams? I would like to know whether the Minister of Public Works is aware that that is the stand taken by the organ of the government in East Pictou.
I am not aware of the stand taken by the paper referred to, nor am I aware that it is the organ of the government or that this government has any organ.
The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) would hardly agree with the minister there.
The expenditure is not very great. The total is only $3,000. The clock will cost $1,200 and the alterations of the building $1,495.

The amount may not look very big, but it is sufficient to supply a daily mail to Bauline, which has now only one mail a week, and it would give it a daily mail for two years.
Pictou Public . Building-Renewals and repairs, $2,000.

Of this amount, $1,500 is a revote. It is to make provision to replace the old galvanized iron roof, which was found leaking, also to re-cover the roof and repair the gable. The tender was for $1,900 and the contingencies $100, making a total of $2,000.
Shelburne Public Building, $19,000.

This was placed under contract February 12, 1908. The building is of stone. It is 39 by 54 feet, two and a half stories high, with a turret three stories high. It is required for a post office and custom house. The total estimated cost, including site, heating, wiring, etc., is $35,158.77.
What is the population of the town?
It is one of the oldest towns in Nova Scotia. Its population was 1,445 seven years ago. Since then it has been connected by railway with other parts of the province, and is now progressing.
Was it in February, 1908 you decided to build that?
The contract was entered into then.
What is the revenue?

The postal revenue is $1,669, customs duties, $1,471, money or-, ders given, $29,439, money orders paid $19,-
000.	The exports are $33,174.
That amounts to $25 per head for every man, woman and child for the total population.

That is a very expensive building for such a place with such a small revenue. I presume that the minister, as a business man, must have some kind of system governing the erection of these buildings in different parts of the country.' I would like to know if other places with an equal revenue are equally entitled to a public building, and if places which have a revenue three or four tmes that amount will be given public buildings?
Places with the population and of the importance of this would have very strong claims on the government. That is as far as my hon. friend can expect me to go.
In whose riding is this?

In that of the Minister of Finance.
Westville Public Building, $5,000.
How big is this place?
It had a population of about 2,300 in 1901 but has increased a good deal since. It is quite a mining centre.
What is the estimated cost?
The building site heating, electric wiring, &c., will cost $25,605.
From whom was the site purchased?
The Acadia Coal Company.
Is it the intention to put a side-walk along the building?

If a side-walk is required, I would favourably regard the suggestion.
Georgetown Public. Building, Prince Edward Island, $7,000.

This building was purchased at a low price, and this amount is

required for alterations to fit it for a public building.
When was it purchased?
In March 1908. The price for building and site was $2,500.
From whom was it purchased?

From E. B. Hessian.
St. John Dominion Building, New Brunswick-improvements, repairs, &c., $4,000.
. Mr. PUGSLEY. This is to make repairs in the St. John Post Office and Custom House and West Side Post Office.
St. John Drill hall, New Brunswick, $12,500.
This is estimated sufficient to pay for the property which the Crown is expropriating as a site for a drill hall. We do not intend this year proceeding with the building.

Why not?
. Mr. PUGSLEY. In pursuance of the policy of postponing for a short time the works with regard to which tenders were not called before the decision was arrived at.
What negotiations have taken place with regard to any expropriation of land in St. John for drill hall purposes?

Instead of negotiating we thought it better to file a plan of expropriation. In that locality many of the titles are somewhat uncertain, and it is not known who are the owners. It is thought better to file a plan of expropriation, and then negotiate afterwards. ' If we cannot arrive at a fair arrangement, we can let the Exchequer Court determine the value.
Is it the intention of the government, or the department, to put through these expropriation proceedings this year?	; ,

Yes.
Public Works-Chargeable to Income-Public Buildings, Quebec-Cookshire Post Office, $15,000.
Would the minister please tell us the particulars of this?

This building is being erected on a lot of land given as a free site by the municipal council of the town. It is a fine lot with a frontage of 100 feet on Main _ street and a depth of 125 feet. The building will be two stories high, and will be of brick on a concrete foundation. The building is required for post office, customs and inland revenue. The total estimated cost, including heating, electric wiring, fittings and furniture, is $23,053.55.
Joliette Armoury, $15,000.
We would like some information about this.

The site upon which this building is to be constructed has a frontage of 100 feet with a depth of 100 feet. The bulding will be of two stories, of brick, on a stone foundation, with stone trimmings, the size being 56 feet by 47 feet. The total estimated cost, including heating, fixtures and furniture, but not including the site, is $21,719.
Has the contract been let?
Yes.
When was it let?

I have not the date here, but it was let quite recently. Six tenders were received in answer to an advertisement, the tenders ranging from $13,500 to $15,395. The lowest was accepted on authority of an order in council passed on January 18 last. But there was some delay in letting the contract.
That was subsequent to the determination of the minister not to proceed with any public works for which contracts were not let? .
No, not subsequently.

That is to say, then, the minister's policy on this subject was adopted subsequent to January 18 of this
year?
Tenders had been called for this building in 1908, and the decision that we arrived at was only arrived at in December.
Why the delay in deciding on the tenders?
I will make inquiries. I think we called twice for tenders.

When was the last call
for tenders?
My deputy tells me that I am in error in saying that there were two calls for tender. There was delay while we were making inquiry as to the responsibility and experience of the contractors.
How large a place is Joliette?
Seven or eight years ago it had a population of 4,200.
Is it about the same yet, or is it larger?

I am told that it is about
6,000	population now.

The hon. minister will remember that in his estimates last year an appropriation was made for an armoury in the city of Portage la Prairie, a city with a population larger than even the population estimated by the minister for

Joliette. But I do not see any appropriation this year for that armoury although it was promised by the candidate who opposed me in the last contest that an armoury would be erected in the city of Portage la Prairie. The reason I asked the minister when that policy was decided upon is that I would like to get at what the reason was for calling for tenders for certain of these public works immediately prior to, or immediately subsequent to, the election, and not calling for tenders for others equally necessary or more necessary for the country.

A large number of buildings were provided for in the Appropriation Act of last year. My directions to the chief architect were to proceed as rapidly as possible to get the plans and specifications ready and to call for tenders just as soon as this was done. But the hon. member will realize that this work takes time, and that plans and specifications for all these public works could not be gone on with at the same time. No selection was made of one place more than another, so far as I am aware. The chief architect went on in the regular way, intending to get out plans in reasonable time and to call for tenders for all these works. The decision arrived at with regard to dropping a large number of the public works was arrived at when we began to prepare the estimates for this session, some time in December, and I think the latter part of December.

Many tenders were called for subsequent to the 26th of October and prior to the date in December when the policy of the minister was decided upon. Then, I can quite understand what governed the department in calling for tenders in some cases and not in others.
What military corps will probably use this Joliette armoury?
This is headquarters for the 83rd Joliette Begiment and of A company.

The minister tells us that the chief architect had instructions to make up the plans and specifications, but that all could not be made up at once. What system is adopted to decide which should be first? Did he commence in the west and go east, or in the middle, or how? Is there any system?

The practice is to follow the estimates that are voted, taking one after the other. Of course, we must first see that sites are obtained. Sometimes it happens that urgent representations are made by a member asking that the site be purchased as soon as possible, otherwise the option might be lost; or he might urge the erection of a building, and Mr. MEIGHEN.
his representations would be heeded. In some towns the necessity of a public building is more urgent than in others. In some places there may be no accommodation for a post office or custom house. All these considerations necessarily weigh in deciding the action of the department.
To whom was the contract given for this work?

Simoneau & Dion, of
Sherbrooke.
After the Public Works Department has completed an armoury, how soon afterwards is it handed over to the Militia Department?
In ordinary course it would be passed over to the Militia Department immediately on completion.
Who were the other tenderers, and what were the prices?
I cannot give the names. There were six tenders, ranging from $13,500 to $15,095.
When was the land purchased, and from whom?
I have not the name here, but I will get it.
Am I correct in understanding that in the matter of calling for tenders the minister exercises a discretion as to what public buildings tenders shall be called for?

I repeat what I have said, that in the ordinary course the chief architect takes the votes as they appear in the appropriation. But sometimes it occurs that a member writes to me urging me to proceed as rapidly as possbile with the erection of a building in a certain place for which there is an appropriation, urging that it is very much needed. I would send a memorandum to the chief architect to hurry along the plans and specifications for the building in such and such a place.

If it is left to the chief architect, and he simply follows the appropriations, I do not think the government would be justified in adopting such an arbitrary line as has been adopted, namely
roceeding with such buildings as tenders
ave been called for and leaving others; because it would result in this, that those provinces that happen to be first in the estimates would secure practically all their public buildings, and those that happened to be last would get none at all. Am I correct in understanding that many tenders were called for subsequent to the 26th of October, and prior to this day in December when the policy of the ministry was decided upon that has borne so harshly on many constituencies throughout Canada?

I thought I had made myself plain. In a number of cases I have been urged to see what was the cause of the delay in getting out plans and specifications. I have urged the chief architect to hurry along the. work and the plans and specifications, but I never interfered with his proceedings or plans. He had a free hand for all buildings for which appropriations were made at the last session of parliament. Quite a number of tenders were called for during the summer. Parliament did not rise until the 20th of July; that accounts for delay in respect to a good many buildings. Later on when we came to consider the estimates and to weigh the revenue and expenditure for the coming year, we decided that in the public interest we would be obliged to drop a large number of public works. Now if I had undertaken to go through the list of buildings throughout Canada and determine which building should be carried on and which should be stopped, it would have been a very difficult task indeed, because when I put the items in the estimates of last year for these buildings I thought they were all necessary in the public interest, and that remark applies as well to buildings in constituencies which were represented by hon. gentlemen opposite as to buildings in constituencies which were represented by our friends. We thought the better way would be to draw the line as clearly as possible between buildings in regard to which tenders had been called for before we reached that decision, and those in regard to which tenders had not been called for. We did not feel that any great injustice was being done to those places with regard to which we were leaving buildings out of the estimates this year, because it did not mean, and does not mean, an abandonment of those buildings; it only means, as we hope, a postponment of them until next year. Parliament will meet in the ordinary course next fall, and then provision can be made, we hope, for the erection of buildings which were left out of the estimates for this year. I am sure that upon reflection my hon. friend, as other hon. members of this House, will see that we have adopted the wisest course. I was compelled, in yielding to the views of my colleagues, particularly my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, to drop some $8,000,000 from my estimates. I was sorry to do it. It has disappointed our hon. friend on this side more than it has disappointed my hon. friend who has just taken his seat. We had to do it. We thought we were doing it in the public interest and the public will justify^ it. We felt that the public would recognize that in taking this step public men are showing their willingness to meet conditions which have come temporarily upon us and which, we hope, will soon pass away. We feel
that the financiers of the world will approve of the course which we have taken because it shows a determination on the part of the government to keep the expenditure within the revenue, and I trust my hon. friend will accept this explanation and allow this item to pass.

The public necessities.

Yes. Of course if I were convinced that any work was not

As at present advised I do not see any reason for changing my mind that all the works provided for last session are necessary public works. Perhaps the Minister of Customs will tell me whether he intends to make Lachute a port of entry seeing that he has now a building there to accommodate his officers?

The building is a very good building, but it was put in the wrong place, and were I to speak about that it might take considerable of the time of the committee. Lachute is exactly in the same position as Alexandria, being half way between Ottawa and Montreal. It is a town of about the same size and yet Alexandria was made a port of entry some years ago. chute, but should I yield, it will be a double argument for some other place and so I will need a little time to think it over.

(Translation.) Mr. Chairman, for the benefit of my hon. friend I will tell him that the site of this postal station is on St. Catherine east. The amount paid for land is $33,000. It was bought from Mr. Jeannotte, a good Conservative.

I think I must ask this item to stand until the Postmaster General is here to tell us what he intends to do about the reorganization of the postal service in Montreal. A great commercial city like Montreal is entitled to the fullest consideration of parliament with respect to matters of this kind, but we should know what policy the government intends to pursue with respect to granting postal facilities. I heard Sir Wm. Mulock, when Postmaster General, state in this House that the government would provide a postal station about midway between the great rail way stations in Montreal in order to forward promptly to the central post office the mail matter arriving in the city. He gave reasons for declaring this as the policy of the government, but nothing has ever been done in that direction. But we find applied in the city of Montreal a principle which prevails everywhere, and which I think should be put a stop to. That principle is this: A man is elected to this House, and his sole object seems to be to have a public building erected within the limits of his constituency. I say without fear of contradiction that in the majority of cases he is a man we see very little of either in the general work of the House or in the very important work of the committees of the House; but he seems to think that if he gets a public building for his constituency that will make up for all his shortcomings; and that public building js erected to suit his caprice, very often in the wrong place, very often, we must admit, unnecessarily, and very often where the money might be spent more advantageously in a different manner. Take, for instance, the city of Montreal, the commercial centre of the Dominion, which contributes one-fifth, if not a larger proportion, of the total revenue of the country. While spending lavishly, if

necessary, in that city, we should apply the money in the best possible way. We have in Montreal a port by far the most important of all the ports in the Dominion. Its income exceeds by an immense amount the income of any other port. For some years we have had there three excellent harbour commissioners, who are doing the best they can for the money they have, and for five years we have had before us the report of the Transportation Commission recommending, as among the foremost necessities of the country, the nationalization of the port of Montreal and the construction of a dry dock there as absolutely essential and urgent. That report, it is true, mentioned other ports which should be nationalized, but the chairman of the commission, in a letter sent subsequent to his report, insisted particularly on the urgency of the case in Montreal. We find at present-and the papers in the last few days have been full of it-that very far from Montreal becoming a free port, or the announcement being made by the government that the recommendation of that most important commission would be carried our, nothing has been done; and in order to carry out the improvements that are absolutely required in the port of Montreal, large indebtedness has been incurred, and to-day the commissioners find it impossible to continue their work without adding to the burdens of the port. Not only the people of Montreal, but I believe all the people of the province of Quebec, and very many people who are interested elsewhere, would say, if they were questioned on the subject, that the very first expense to be incurred should be in the direction of carrying out the recommendation of the Transportation Commission and making the port of Montreal a free port. With the competition of the American ports, the idea of adding to the burdens of the port of Montreal, embarrassing commerce and putting us on a retrograde march instead of enabling us to go forward, would be condemned by everybody. Quite lately the Board of Trade of Montreal has taken the matter up exactly as I have stated it to the House. The government seems to be indifferent to that very question. Therefore, it is important for us to know if the construction of all these postal stations is necessary. If it is, I have not a word to say. But this policy varies entirely from the policy of the government as I heard it laid down not many years ago by Sir William Mulock, speaking in this House on behalf of the government. In Montreal we have a somewhat strange phenomenon. The postal revenue of that city, the largest in the Dominion, is considerably less than that of the city of Toronto. What is the reason of that unexplained difference? To my mind it is attributable to this:	That our

postal system in Montreal requires reform and requires additional expenditure. Our post office is properly manned. Our officers, whether the superior officers or those who have charge of the delivery of letters, perform their duties well; but they are absolutely insufficient in number; they are scandalously underpaid and they have not the means of giving us a proper service. I have made suggestions already, and I will make them again when the postal estimates come up, because I believe that if we applied ourselves to correct these deficiencies, and if w# had in Montreal such a postal delivery as there is in other large cities- in London, in Paris, perhaps in Toronto- so that if a letter is put in a postal box at a certain hour it is sure to be delivered at a certain hour, the revenue of the Montreal post office would swell by leaps and bounds, and would soon equal if not surpass that of the city of Toronto. There is not that confidence at the present moment. Therefore, I ask is it wise for us to expend such a large amount of money in building postal stations, and could not the money be better applied in other ways? I think we should be informed by the Postmaster General if this way of spending money is the result of a settled policy of the government-the policy of erecting public buildings for the satisfaction of members representing different constituencies, in order that they may have the opportunity to show their electors that they have done something for their respective constituencies. It would be wiser for us to improve our postal system than to build large postal stations without improvements.
I think, in view of what is happening to our harbour commission, in view of the very large amount-an amount which I cannot understand, and which appears to be highly excessive-which we are spending on the central post office-a sum which, when we have finished with that post office, will amount to over $700,000-in view of these expenditures, it is wise for the committee to pause and ask the Postmaster General if this is the result of a policy and if we cannot make better use of our money than to build a larger number of these postal stations. What is essential to a postal service is not to build postal stations unless absolutely necessary in order to insure what is absolutely required in a commercial city like Montreal, namely, an efficient postal service.
this postal station was required by all the electors of that constituency, whose number exceeds 48,000 inhabitants.
In that part of the city the postal business are of great importance. I will only mention the case of Mr. Filion, an apothecary, living in the north part of St. Mary's division who last year has made $93,000 in a small office of some square feet in size.
St. Mary's division forms one of the most commercial wards in the city of Montreal. St. Catherine street, from east to west; Notre Dame street from east to west, Ontario and Craig streets are nearly exclusively filled up with commercial firms. The large manufacturers are situated in that constituency.
Let me mention by the way, Sir, a few of those manufactures which are built there: A great number of breweries, some manufactures of shirts and glass works. We count also a manufacture of oilcloth, another one of engines, two of caoutchouc, a part of cotton mills, a manufacture of paints, without reckoning the largest tobacco manufacture of our Dominion, the Macdonald manufacture, and also the Dominion Tobacco Company. We have a few others more. A sugar refinery, some manufactures of cigars, thread, biscuits, shoes, sash and doors, with many others whose enumeration would be tedious.
If I have used every endeavour to obtain a postal station in that constituency it was not for the purpose of making easy my reelection, because the hon. member knows the majority which I won in 1906. If I have attempted to induce the government to give us that postal station it was because I knew it was indispensable. If the revenue of Ontario is considerably larger than that of Quebec-I mean the postal revenue-it is because the first one is better provided with postal stations which afford more facilities to the citizens in view of transacting postal business. I think my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier has been mistaken when he said it was a caprice of the member for St. Mary's. I will repeat again that I did not want that postal station in order to be re-elected. I have given sufficient proof of that. I want to add that the Conservative members are always ready to object to some estimate of the province of Quebec. It is not the same thing about the estimates of the province of Ontario.

Yes. From sub-stations A and B there is every kind of delivery just as from the central post office. Mr. GERVAIS There are three kinds of districts; there are the remote districts, which are supposed to get three deliveries per day; then there are the sub-postal station districts which are supposed to receive four to six daily deliveries; then there is the commercial centre of Montreal properly speaking, which is bounded by Craig street, the river, Wellington street and Bonsecours market, which district is supposed to get about an hourly delivery, that is about eight deliveries per day. Exactly. For example, in each sub-postal station there are head-

quarters lor letter carriers. There are three groups of letter carriers. $50 a year, on an average.

tre, upon the same basis.
