I now enter this request of the minister and of the government generally, to the effect that if you are to endow the different sections of the city of Montreal with these postal distributing stations, the first district to be endowed should be the Chaboillez Square district, which gives tc-day the second largest revenue of all the 52 stations.

The question of distance for distribution is a very important one. What is the distance between Cha-boiliez Square and the central post office? Not more than three-quarters of a mile. We have some sub-postal stations that have only been in operation for one year and a half. I think it is a proof of its necessity if, after one year and a half we are getting now a revenue of over $11,000 from a subpost office. Let me tell my hon. friend from St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) that his constituency has been princely served, because the total cost of sub-postal station A, right in the heart of his constituency, has cost over $200,000. I may say that before a couple of years are past, the revenue of the sub-postal station B, in St. Catherine street and Amherst street will exceed the revenue of the sub-postal station in the district of the hon. member for St. Antoine.	.
The hon. member for St. Antoine will, I suppose, concede that there is a tremendous amount of business being done daily upon St. Catherine street, between Visita-

tion street and St. Lawrence Main. The grand total of the business in St. James division is as great as that on St. Catherine street within the boundary of St. Antoine division. The hon. member for St. Antoine should not expect to have his protest considered very seriously by this government. I do not know at whose request he has been enjoying the good will of the government to the amount of a quarter of a million dollars without any more benefit than the government is getting from the sub-station building at Amherst and St. Catherine streets. I understand that the government is not paying more than $1,500 rent for the building used as a sub-postal station at Amherst and St. Catherine streets, which is not to be compared with the interest which the government is paying on the quarter of a million it has spent for the building of the monumental sub postal station at University and St. Catherine streets west. I think, therefore, that this committee can well disregard any protest made on behalf of the hon. member for St. Antoine.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that the whole question is a question of distance from the central post office and that the- business to be attended to has nothing to do with it?
Yes, it has.

How does the hon. gentleman explain that this rented establishment that produces this income of $13,000 a year is to be treated as of less consequence than an establishment that produces $3,000 a year? He tells my hon. friend from St. Antoine that the government has spent $200,000 in his division. Does the hon. gentleman know that this particular post office producing this large revenue is in the division of St. Ann and will he tell us what monumental generosity the government bestowed upon that division?

In St. James division the government has not spent more than $5,000 per year for the maintenance of Amherst street sub-postal station, although that sub-postal station has given as large a revenue as the Chaboillez Square postal station. The distance between Amherst street sub-postal station and the central post office is about double the distance between the sub-postal office and Chaboillez Square in St. Ann's division. I am not against the establishment or maintenance of a postal station on Chaboillez Square. I am in favour of the establishment of as many sub-postal stations as possible, taking into consideration the question of business and revenue.

Just one word more and that is to ask the minister if he will be 42
good enough, in the course of this present year, and before he comes to the House again with further estimates for additional sub-postal stations in Montreal, to give to this matter of the sub-postal stations in our city some serious consideration as to where they should be placed, and determine that their location may not be based simply upon the needs of a single constituency or upon the demands of two or three members of this House. All that we ask is that the minister shall look upon the city of Montreal from a business point of view. Here lies a city stretching four miles in one direction by three miles in another. In the centre is the main post office. If we are going to have sub-distribution stations how many should we establish, three, four, five or six, or whatever number is necessary to meet the needs of the case? If we decide that we are to establish four, where shall we place them? Let there be a definite policy, so that it may be understood when we are building1 this one to-day that one will be built to-morrow, this one a year after, and that one in a subsequent year; so that we may feel that the entire city of Montreal, having an equal claim upon the government, is epuitably treated and a complete system is evolved in consequence. Otherwise, we find that it becomes the practice for a member representing the division, particularly on the government side, to make before the electors great promises as to securing them a post office, and then, having secured the appropriation, he endeavours to put that post office in a place that will be most useful to that particular entourage without reference to the interests of the city as a whole. These post offices should be placed not with reference to ward boundaries, but with reference to the needs of the districts which they are to serve, and I hope the minister will take thati matter up with the expectation of giving' the city of Montreal four or five suitably situated postal sub-stations.
That has been the policy of the government.
No, they have got them all in this half of the city.
Because the business is there, always going more and more to the east of Montreal.
No, while they have done that the largest revenue with one exception comes from the Chaboillez Square section.

These stations are all built on the recommendation of the Postmaster General by the Department of Public Works, and that is why I think it would have been more satisfactory if we had had a statement of a general system adopted by the government and an explanation of



a plan applicable to the whole city of Montreal from the Postmaster General, because the Minister of Public Works is not in a position to give us that information. As far as Montreal is concerned there is no idea whatever of differentiating between the east and west. The hon. member for St. Mary's (Mr. Martin) will, I think, admit that readily. What we want is an efficient postal system. I think that in Toronto, they are more exacting upon that points Our only desire is that we should have our rights in this matter. We ask that in the city of Montreal you will give us an efficient postal system with sure and certain delivery. Although the employees do their very best, and although they are most efficient, there is no certainty that a letter posted at an important business place in the eastern part of the city, at the Angus shops, for instance, will reach its destination in time.
They have a sub-post office there.

There is no certainty, I say, that the letter will be delivered at Point St. Charles at a certain hour. The hon. member for St. James (Mr. Gervais) knows it very well. There are drop letter boxes and there is something marked on the boxes as to the hour at which the next collection will be made. That mark is almost always obliterated from the box. I have never seen it so in the city of Toronto. It is important, when you drop a letter in the box, that the signs should be there in order that you may know exactly when the last collection was made and when the next one will be made. These things appear to be trifling details, but my hon. friend knows they are very important and if we have a service there equal to what they have in Toronto you will see an increase in the postal revenue in Montreal which will carry us far beyond the revenue at present obtained in Toronto, which is the largest revenue in the Dominion. Does my hon. friend from St. Mary's (Mr. Martin) think it is unpatriotic to plead for that?
They are doing it in the province of Ontario through Mr. Ross and in Quebec now.

I am very glad to hear that. With regard to postal stations I may say that a suitable and ornamental sub-station could be erected cheaper than is the case under the present system, and if we are to have many of these we should see that they are all of the same model as is the case irt the United States where you can recognize the sub-postal station buildings from afar. It should not be the rule that the building in St. Mary's division should be a very fine and costly one because the member representing that division is an influential and Mr. MONK.
big man, and that another division just as important though not so influentially represented should have a smaller building. If the minister gives me the occasion -tct tender I will undertake to build such postal stations as I have suggested for far less money then he is now spending, and I shall be able to retire with a competency.

My hon. friend (Mr. Monk) is always eloquent but he has not explained the conditions in the central post office in Montreal. That post office has practically been doing the postal business of the greater part of Canada, and the officials there have been sorting the incoming European mail to the advantage of the employees of the Toronto office. Should the plan be carried out of sorting the European mail on the ocean steamers the officials of the Montreal post office will have more time to attend to local business. I think myself that the Toronto office should do the sorting and distribution for Winnipeg and the west.
Then there is something wrong in the system.
I have no right to speak for the government, but from my; point of view I think the present system is not a perfect one and can be improved.
I think my hon. friend (Mr. Gervais) is qualifying for the office of Postmaster General.
I was in Montreal last Sunday and I desired at six o'clock to mail a letter for the train which leaves Windsor station at 7.25, but I was informed that the mail had been closed.

I would point out to the hon. gentleman that under the new Sabbath Observance law it is forbidden even to the officials of the government that they should work on Sunday, except on very urgent business.

Will the minister lay on the table of the House at his earliest convenience a statement showing the boundaries of the districts to be served by each of the two sub-stations for which a vote is asked in these estimates?
I will be very glad to ask the Postmaster General for that.

We must have a horse before we build a stable and the Post Office Department must wait for the business to grow before it erects post offices, so that it is idle to ask for a plan of what may be done in the future, in districts of the Montreal Island where there is no business today.
